title: Dengue Out break Sri Lanka
summary: LKA: Epidemic - 07-2026 - Dengue Out break Sri Lanka #2 (2026-07-16)
description: The signs of escalation set out in BEACON's report on 03 Jul 2026 have now been met: high-risk MOH divisions have expanded beyond 124 (now 175); the case fatality rate (CFR) has risen above the 0.05% historical baseline (now 0.07%); and case counts have not declined in July. The timing is the central concern. The southwest monsoon peak was expected to wane by mid-July, yet week 27 produced the highest weekly total of the year, with 44 newly designated high-risk areas. An epidemic curve that continues to accelerate as its principal seasonal driver recedes indicates that transmission is being sustained by factors that will not resolve with the rainfall and that the curve has not yet reached its apex. Gampaha's displacement of Colombo as the leading district is analytically significant rather than incidental. Gampaha is the district with documented insecticide resistance in Aedes aegypti and Ae albopictus populations, and its emergence as the national epicenter is consistent with reduced efficacy of the fogging and adulticide components of the current response. This implies that the intensified vector-control campaign may be delivering diminishing returns precisely where the burden is now heaviest. The university clusters introduce a transmission setting that was absent in earlier phases of the outbreak. Campuses concentrate exposure in communal outdoor and shared-accommodation environments during daytime hours. Student mobility across districts creates a plausible mechanism for onward seeding, particularly if campus closures disperse cohorts to home districts. Whether school and university reopenings generate further institutional clusters is a near-term indicator to monitor. Comparative analysis and future outlook As of 10 Jul 2026, the year-to-date total of 67 143 cases has already surpassed the full-year totals of recent endemic years, including the 51 000 cases reported in 2025. At the current rate of roughly 1100 cases per day, the 100 000-case projection in BEACON's report on 23 Jun 2026 would be reached in mid-August, before the October–December northeast monsoon peak begins. On that trajectory, the 2019 epidemic (105 049 reported cases) is no longer a distant comparator but a plausible outcome of the current monsoon season alone. The critical determinant of the 2026 total is therefore not the current peak but the August–September inter-monsoon trough. Sri Lanka has historically seen incidence decline between the two monsoon peaks; if that decline does not occur, the country will enter the northeast monsoon season with a saturated hospital system, an expanded high-risk geography, and a partially immune population exposed to a dominant serotype.
actions: SLRCS is planning to revise the ongoing DREF appeal as per the request made by the National Dengue Control Unit.
recommendations: Scale up vaccination campaigns and immunization coverage.; Enhance disease surveillance and laboratory testing capacities.

title: Flooding as a result of Typhoon Maysak
summary: LAO: Flood - 07-2026 - Flooding as a result of Typhoon Maysak #4 (2026-07-14)
description: Following Typhoon Maysak, which brought several days of moderate-to-heavy rainfall beginning on 2 July 2026, widespread flooding affected multiple parts of the Lao PDR. The combined effects of flash floods, river flooding, landslides and prolonged inundation caused significant damage to housing, agriculture, transportation infrastructure, livelihoods, and other community assets across Luang Namtha, Bokeo, Phongsali, Vientiane, Bolikhamxai, Khammouane, and Savannakhet provinces. According to the Lao National Disaster Management Committee (NDMC), four provinces, five districts and 28 villages were affected. A total of 3,822 households, representing approximately 21,067 people, including 8,217 women, were impacted by the flooding. Khammouane Province was among the worst-affected areas, particularly Nakai and Koun Kham districts, where flooding resulted in evacuations, damage to residential areas and agricultural land, and disruption to transportation and essential services. In Koun Kham District, 14 households were evacuated to temporary shelters, while additional stranded travellers were accommodated by local authorities. Although floodwaters have begun to recede in some areas, damage assessments remain ongoing. Government authorities and humanitarian partners continue to monitor the situation and identify priority recovery needs, including food assistance, safe drinking water, agricultural inputs and support for vulnerable households.
actions: The Lao Red Cross (LRC) National Headquarters has instructed its Disaster Management Office and provincial branches to closely monitor the evolving situation and coordinate with disaster management committees at all levels to support affected communities. Provincial and district Red Cross branches have conducted rapid assessments, coordinated with local authorities to identify humanitarian needs and regularly reported updates to the National Headquarters. In Khammouane Province, the Provincial Red Cross and Nakai District Red Cross installed an AP700 water treatment unit in Na Hang Village on 8 July 2026 to provide safe drinking water to flood-affected communities. LRC is continuing detailed assessments to identify households with significant losses and plans to provide cash-based assistance during the recovery phase based on assessment findings. Many of the affected villages are located within the SAFER Project, which is supported by the Swiss Red Cross (SRC). LRC is working with project partners to utilize available emergency response resources, conduct detailed needs assessments, and integrate recovery planning with planned Enhanced Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (EVCA) activities where appropriate.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
summary: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
description: Bangladesh is experiencing widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across the south-eastern and north-eastern regions of the country. Although the low-pressure system that triggered the initial period of extreme rainfall has weakened and moved towards Uttar Pradesh, India, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) continues to forecast intermittent heavy to very heavy rainfall through 13 July across the divisions of Chattogram, Sylhet, Rangpur, Rajshahi, Dhaka, Khulna, and Barishal. While rainfall intensity is expected to gradually decrease in the coming days, the risk of further flooding and landslides remains elevated. Rainfall has remained exceptionally high. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf recorded 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm) and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm). Additional rainfall of 100–300 mm was forecast through 12 July, maintaining a high risk of flooding, waterlogging and landslides. Flood conditions continue to evolve. As of 11 July, several river stations remained above danger level, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu and Khowai rivers. By the evening of 11 July, seven stations on five rivers across six districts were flowing above danger level. The Sangu River in Bandarban exceeded danger level by more than two metres at its peak, while rising river levels continue to threaten low-lying areas in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh and northern river basins. The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,074,534 people have been affected across 10 districts . The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people have been temporarily displaced , while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters have been opened. Government reporting indicates that more than 267,918 households have been stranded or cut off by floodwaters across seven districts, while media reports citing the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief indicate that at least 51 people have died nationwide due to floods and landslides. Preliminary Government reports indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban and 13,860 in Chattogram . The full extent and severity of housing damage remain unclear, as standing water and access constraints continue to delay detailed assessments. Water, sanitation and hygiene ( WASH ) services have been disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts . In several areas, infrastructure remains submerged, while water sources have been damaged or contaminated by floodwater carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering ( DPHE ) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 waterpoints had been fully or partially damaged . The most affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and host communities. Across the 33 camps affected more than 28,000 people , damaged over 3,100 shelters were damaged, more than 4,700 individuals were displaced , and caused multiple fatalities and injuries associated with landslides and flooding. UNHCR has reported 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees and thousands of people left homeless following landslides and shelter collapse. The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has activated a multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected populations across the impacted districts. Emergency measures include the opening of more than 1,000 shelters, the allocation and distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water and other relief items, and the deployment of the Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation and relief operations. The Government has deployed 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas. Government authorities continue to monitor the evolving situation through national and district-level coordination mechanisms, while prioritizing assistance to the most severely affected areas, including Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Efforts are ongoing to maintain access to essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian needs in affected communities.
actions: The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) has activated its central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and is coordinating response efforts across flood- and landslide-affected districts in south-eastern and north-eastern Bangladesh. Continuous information collection, situation monitoring, and coordination with district units, government authorities, IFRC, and humanitarian partners are ongoing. BDRCS has mobilized emergency resources through a combination of internal funds and partner support. A total of BDT 1.8 million has been released to district units in Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj to support immediate response activities. To strengthen evacuation and rescue capacity, BDRCS mobilized emergency rescue equipment and non-food items including: 12 rubber boats, 110 life jackets, 135 rescue helmets, 135 rescue boots, 145 pairs of gloves, 5 generators, 5,500 jerrycans, Rescue ropes, rope bags, float plates and rescue panels. BDRCS has provided emergency food assistance to 2,220 flood-affected households across Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Food packages included rice, puffed rice, lentils, oil, salt, sugar, drinking water, biscuits, ORS, soap, sanitary pads and other essential items. In Cox's Bazar, through the Population Movement Operation (PMO), BDRCS continues to support Rohingya refugees and host communities through supporting early warning dissemination, emergency relocation, search and rescue, and coordination through Camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs) and humanitarian partners across all 33 camps. BDRCS PMO has provided emergency shelter assistance to 494 affected households in Camps 11 and 12, while WASH volunteers are assessing damaged facilities and coordinating with sector partners. Health teams continue community outreach, referrals, household visits, and essential health services, including outpatient and maternity care. Through its volunteers and field teams, BDRCS remains actively engaged in addressing the immediate needs of flood- and landslide-affected refugees and host communities, BDRCS called an emergency coordination meeting on 12 July with IFRC, ICRC and in-country Participating National Societies to update about the overall flood situation and response by BDRCS. Based on needs, BDRCS is also planning to scale-up operation by mobilizing: Mobile Water Treatment Plants, emergency medical teams, essential household items and cash assistance. Based on the initial damage and needs assessments, BDRCS requested IFRC on 8 July 2026 to support the launch of a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation targeting populations affected by floods and landslides in the Rohingya camps and adjacent host communities in Cox’s Bazar. The proposed operation aims to address urgent humanitarian needs through life-saving interventions, including early warning dissemination, evacuation support, search and rescue, emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, cash and voucher assistance (CVA), volunteer mobilization, and operational coordination. The DREF operation is intended to complement ongoing response efforts by BDRCS and humanitarian partners while strengthening support to the most vulnerable and affected communities.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Algeria: Wildfires – July 2026
summary: DZA: Fire - 07-2026 - Algeria: Wildfires – July 2026
description: On 18 July 2026, the wildfire emergency in Algeria reached a significant operational peak, with 154 forest, vegetation and agricultural fires recorded within 24 hours across several wilayas. Of these, 138 fires were extinguished, while 16 remained active at the time of reporting. The fires affected northern, north-eastern, central and western Algeria, including Annaba, Souk Ahras, Skikda, Guelma, Bouira, Médéa, Mila, Mascara, El Tarf, Jijel, Sétif, Béjaïa, Tlemcen, Saïda, Tissemsilt, Biskra and Chlef. Over the last 24 hours, the Ministry of the Interior, Local Authorities and Transport confirmed six fatalities linked to the wildfires. In Seraïdi, Annaba, more than 100 patients were evacuated from a rehabilitation hospital, while approximately 150 homes were affected or threatened. Preventive evacuations were also carried out in several localities, including El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira. The Government of Algeria has led a strong and coordinated national response, ensuring the rapid mobilization of the competent authorities and emergency services. Efforts have focused on protecting lives, supporting affected communities, securing threatened areas and maintaining close operational coordination across the affected wilayas. The Algerian Red Crescent mobilized its provinces committees, volunteers and logistical resources from the beginning of the emergency. Teams provided first aid, drinking water, food assistance, psychosocial support and essential humanitarian assistance to affected communities and emergency responders. Response and monitoring activities continue, while high temperatures, dry vegetation, difficult terrain and the risk of fire re-ignition remain important operational considerations.
actions: Incident assessment, stakeholder coordination, mitigation measures, monitoring and post-incident review.
recommendations: Establish fire management committees and community-based fire prevention networks.; Establish fire prevention and control training programs.; Develop community fire breaks and firebreaks in wildfire-prone areas.

title: Severe Storms
summary: URY: Other - 07-2026 - Severe Storms #2 (2026-07-21)
description: According to Uruguay's National Emergency System (SINAE), severe storms affected much of the country between July 16 and 18, 2026, with wind gusts of up to 129.5 km/h recorded in the department of Salto, the most affected. The event caused one confirmed death, one person injured and four evacuations, and left more than 37,800 homes without electricity nationwide, with Salto and Maldonado being the hardest hit departments. In the city of Salto, strong winds knocked down trees and power lines and ripped roofs off numerous homes; local authorities (CECOED Salto) report that one locality remains practically isolated, affecting approximately 90 families. Heavy rains continued until July 20, with accumulated rains of between 150 and 225 mm recorded in the departments of Durazno, Florida and Treinta y Tres. According to the National Water Directorate (DINAGUA), several watersheds, including the Yí, Cuareim and Olimar Grande rivers, have rising levels, with flood alerts in force until July 23-24 for areas of Durazno, Artigas and Treinta y Tres. On July 20, the national government declared an agricultural emergency in Salto after the Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries (MGAP) confirmed that 300 producers, 85% of those registered with the General Directorate of the Farm, were affected, with damage to approximately 300 hectares of crops. President Yamandú Orsi visited the affected area. Local authorities and the state-owned power company UTE are continuing restoration operations and assistance to the affected population, much of whom remains without adequate shelter .
actions: The Uruguayan Red Cross has not implemented response actions so far. The National Society activated its monitoring teams to follow up on the evolution of the event (impact of the storm in Salto and other departments, and the hydrological situation in development in the basins of the Yí, Cuareim and Olimar Grande rivers), and is evaluating the possible need for intervention.
recommendations: Conduct rapid needs assessment and impact evaluation.; Activate emergency coordination mechanisms.

title: Nuristan Parun
summary: AFG: Flood - 07-2026 - Nuristan Parun
description: On Monday, 20 July 2026, at approximately 3:00 p.m. local time, a sudden flash flood struck the central areas of Nuristan Province following heavy and continuous rainfall. The low-lying areas and communities located along rivers and seasonal watercourses were the most severely affected. In Nuristan Province, the flash floods resulted in fatalities and injuries, while causing extensive damage to the central market, residential houses, public infrastructure, livelihoods and income sources, as well as agricultural land. This event is part of seasonal flooding currently affecting parts of Nuristan Province, with the most severe impacts reported in Parun District, the provincial capital. Around 85 families have been affected by these floods in Parun, Nuristan. The flash floods caused: 20 people dead 80 people were injured. More than 100 people remain missing. More than 30 houses were damaged, including 7 houses completely destroyed and 23 houses partially damaged In addition, one mosque was destroyed. More than 45 livestock animals were lost. Approximately around 2 jeribs(4000 Square meter) of agricultural land were damaged. (The extent of agricultural damage was limited because the flooding occurred primarily within the city area.) Six vehicles of different types were destroyed. The municipality building was destroyed. A total of seven markets, belonging to both the municipality and private owners, were destroyed. Five hotels and commercial buildings, owned by the municipality and private individuals, were destroyed. Two major public concrete bridges were destroyed. Approximately 2 kilometers of the main public paved road were damaged. Several shops and market stalls were destroyed. A total of 100 meters of retaining walls, two water diversion structures, and three water supply networks were damaged.
actions: Following the flooding, the Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS) immediately mobilized its emergency response teams, deploying more than 70 volunteers and 16 staff members from the Nuristan Provincial Branch. Search and Rescue (SAR) and First Aid teams were rapidly deployed to the affected areas. Coordination was established with the relevant government authorities and health service providers. ARCS has been actively engaged in search and rescue operations, which remain ongoing. Two ambulances have been deployed since the flood occurred to support the transportation of injured and deceased people. since the onset of the flooding, the Afghan Red Crescent Society's (ARCS) fixed clinic staff have been continuously providing medical assistance and treatment to injured people and patients with a medical camp, and these services remain ongoing
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Monsoon Floods Situation Update 3
summary: PAK: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 06-2026 - Monsoon Floods Situation Update 3 #2 (2026-07-21)
description: Since the onset of the 2026 southwest monsoon on 28 June, intermittent to heavy rainfall has affected several parts of Pakistan, significantly increasing the risk of flash floods, riverine flooding, cloudbursts, landslides, urban flooding, thunderstorms, and Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)-related incidents, particularly across northern and mountainous regions. Successive monsoon spells have impacted Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), Punjab, Balochistan, and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), resulting in localized flooding, damage to residential houses and critical infrastructure, disruption of transport and communication networks, and humanitarian impacts in vulnerable districts. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs), and the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) continue to closely monitor the evolving situation and issue regular weather advisories and impact-based forecasts. Between 28 June and 21 July 2026, multiple weather-related incidents were reported from Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Balochistan, and Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The most affected districts included Diamer, Ghizer, Ghanche, Nagar, Astore, Upper Chitral, Lower Chitral, Shangla, Khyber, Lower Dir, Mardan, Rajanpur, Dera Ghazi Khan, Khuzdar, and Neelum. Reported impacts included flash floods, cloudbursts, landslides, damage to residential houses, schools, roads, bridges, irrigation channels, water supply schemes, electricity infrastructure, standing crops, orchards, and other public facilities, resulting in casualties, injuries, displacement, and disruption of essential services. Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs), district administrations, rescue services, and relevant line departments continue to conduct rapid damage assessments, emergency response, and restoration activities in the affected areas. Among the significant incidents reported during the period, a cloudburst on 19 July in Lari Mengal, Doga Top, and Katha Peeran (Union Council Salkhala, Tehsil Athmuqam, District Neelum, AJK) triggered a flash flood that damaged educational institutions, residential houses, commercial shops, and vehicles. Rescue teams and relevant government departments immediately initiated response operations, rapid damage assessments, and the relocation of affected families to safer locations. On the same day, heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding in Rupal Valley, Sub-Division Shounter, District Astore, Gilgit-Baltistan, where no casualties or damage to residential houses were reported, although minor damage to agricultural crops occurred. Subsequently, on 21 July, another flash flood in Louse Village, District Astore, inundated several residential houses, damaging household belongings and essential assets. According to the initial assessment conducted by the District Disaster Management Authority Astore, number of houses were severely affected, and the Gilgit-Baltistan Disaster Management Authority (GBDMA) initiated arrangements for the distribution of emergency relief items while detailed assessments remain ongoing. According to the latest PMD and NDMA weather advisories, active monsoon conditions are expected to persist through 24 July 2026. Moist monsoon currents from the Arabian Sea, supported by a shallow westerly wave, are likely to generate widespread rain with isolated heavy to very heavy falls over Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, northeastern Punjab, and adjoining hilly areas. Localized flash flooding, landslides, cloudbursts, and GLOF-related incidents remain possible, particularly across mountainous and upper catchment areas. Although the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, and Sutlej rivers are currently flowing within normal ranges and no significant riverine flooding is anticipated, authorities continue to closely monitor river flows, rainfall patterns, and vulnerable locations due to the possibility of localized high-impact weather events.
actions: Incident assessment, stakeholder coordination, mitigation measures, monitoring and post-incident review.
recommendations: Establish flash flood detection and real-time alert mechanisms.; Build safe evacuation routes in mountainous and vulnerable communities.

title: Heavy Rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam
summary: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Heavy Rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #3 (2026-07-20)
description: Within minutes on the morning of 17 July, flash floods carrying large volumes of water, mud and debris swept across National Highway 32, inundating homes and posing an immediate threat to lives and property. The floods claimed five lives, while three people remain missing beneath mud and debris. Eight people were injured, and dozens of households were evacuated from high-risk areas as an emergency precaution. The floods affected 53 houses, including 20 houses that were completely washed away. Approximately 300 hectares of rice fields, crops and aquaculture areas were buried or swept away. Several transport routes, irrigation facilities, schools and power systems were also damaged. Although floodwaters have now receded, widespread destruction remains, with many affected households continuing to face the impacts of the disaster. Immediately following the disaster, local authorities activated emergency response measures. Provincial and commune-level Civil Defence Command Committees were deployed to affected areas to coordinate search and rescue operations, restrict access to dangerous roads, and evacuate people from areas at risk of landslides. The province mobilised nearly 1,000 personnel, along with multiple vehicles and equipment, to support disaster response and recovery efforts. The flash floods were triggered by persistent heavy to very heavy rainfall across the northern mountainous region, where cumulative rainfall over the past three days generally ranged from 150–300 mm. The highest accumulations were recorded at Chế Tạo (Lào Cai) with 474 mm, Nậm Păm (Sơn La) with 350 mm, Nà Tấu (Điện Biên) with 277 mm, and Pa Thắng (Lai Châu) with 250 mm. Further rainfall is expected to hamper response and recovery efforts. On 20 July, moderate to heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast across the northern mountainous region and Quảng Ninh Province, with widespread rainfall of 20–50 mm and isolated areas expected to receive more than 100 mm. Short-duration intense rainfall exceeding 70 mm within three hours is possible. Other parts of northern Viet Nam are forecast to experience scattered showers and thunderstorms, with rainfall of 10–20 mm and isolated areas receiving more than 50 mm. According to reports from Lào Cai, Lai Châu, Điện Biên and Sơn La provinces, heavy rainfall, floods, inundation, flash floods and landslides from 15–19 July 2026 caused the following impacts: Human impact: Five people were killed, three remain missing, and 10 people were injured, all reported in Lai Châu Province. Housing: A total of 36 houses collapsed (Lai Châu: 24; Lào Cai: 1; Sơn La: 11); 391 houses were damaged (Lai Châu: 35; Lào Cai: 305; Điện Biên: 27; Sơn La: 24); 140 houses required emergency relocation (Lào Cai: 71; Lai Châu: 26; Điện Biên: 3; Sơn La: 40); and 194 houses were affected by flooding and landslides (Lai Châu: 51; Lào Cai: 65; Điện Biên: 20; Sơn La: 58). Agriculture: A total of 707 hectares of rice and crops were affected (Lào Cai: 76.45 ha; Lai Châu: 409.51 ha; Điện Biên: 27.24 ha; Sơn La: 193.80 ha). Livestock: Approximately 250 livestock and poultry were killed or washed away. Transport infrastructure: Landslides affected multiple sections of roads, including national highways (QL4H, QL12, QL32 and QL279) and provincial roads in Lai Châu (ĐT127, ĐT128, ĐT129, ĐT133, ĐT133B, ĐT134, ĐT135, ĐT138 and ĐT138C); QL279, QL32 and ĐT175B in Lào Cai; 32 locations along ĐT109 in Sơn La; and QL12, QL279 and ĐT143 in Điện Biên, as well as various inter-village and inter-commune roads. title: Measles Outbreak
summary: MWI: Epidemic - 07-2026 - Measles Outbreak
description: The measles outbreak in Nsanje District continues to worsen, affecting several communities, particularly those along the Malawi–Mozambique border. As of 17 July 2026, the district had recorded 188 suspected measles cases, including 76 laboratory-confirmed cases. Children under 15 years of age, particularly those younger than five years, are the most affected. Key drivers of the outbreak include low immunization coverage, delayed health-seeking behaviour, cross-border population movement, and incomplete vaccination records. The situation has escalated in Traditional Authority (T/A) Mbenje, where some members of the Apostolic community do not seek treatment at health facilities due to religious beliefs. Tragically, one child recently died after not being taken to a health facility for medical care. This highlights the urgent need for intensified community engagement, risk communication, and efforts to promote timely healthcare seeking and measles vaccination. The outbreak is placing considerable pressure on the health system through increased demand for disease surveillance, case investigation, laboratory testing, case management, and community outreach. Response efforts continue to be constrained by shortages of essential medical supplies, inadequate transport and fuel, and limited resources to support active surveillance and rapid response activities. The affected population remains at high risk of severe illness, complications, and death, particularly among unvaccinated children. Urgent interventions are needed to strengthen routine and outbreak-response immunization, enhance community awareness, improve cross-border coordination, and ensure timely access to quality healthcare services. From week 1 to week 27 of 2026, a total of 1,690 cumulative Measles alerts were reported with 695 Measles-rubella cases (laboratory-confirmed, epidemiologically linked, and clinically compatible). The laboratory-confirmed cases were distributed across twenty-four (24) districts in the country, with confirmed outbreaks in Balaka, Nsanje and Chikwawa. Additionally, Dedza and Machinga districts have consistently reported measles alerts, warranting further attention.
actions: Since the onset of the measles outbreak, the Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS), through its volunteers, has continued to support the Ministry of Health in implementing community-based outbreak response activities in the affected areas. Volunteers continue supporting Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) activities, including community awareness sessions on measles prevention, early healthcare seeking, the importance of vaccination, and the collection of community feedback to address concerns and rumours. Volunteers also strengthen Community-Based Surveillance (CBS) by identifying and referring suspected measles cases, supporting active case finding, and participating in contact tracing to limit further transmission. In addition, MRCS volunteers provide First Aid services where required and deliver Psychosocial Support Services (PSS) to affected people and their caregivers to help address the emotional and psychological impacts of the outbreak. The National Society also continue to provide operational support to volunteers through coordination and supervision facilitate effective implementation of response activities in the affected communities.
recommendations: Increase routine immunization coverage and outbreak response vaccination campaigns.; Scale up vaccination campaigns and immunization coverage.; Enhance disease surveillance and laboratory testing capacities.

title: Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
summary: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
description: Bangladesh has experienced widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across its south-eastern and north-eastern regions following several days of exceptionally heavy monsoon rainfall. The emergency was initially triggered by a low-pressure system that brought intense rainfall across large parts of the country, resulting in severe flooding, waterlogging, river overflows, and landslides in vulnerable areas. Rainfall totals were particularly high in Chattogram, Teknaf, Bandarban, and Sylhet districts. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm of rainfall on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf received 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm), and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm). Although weather conditions have gradually improved, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecasts that active monsoon conditions will continue through 20 July, bringing light to moderate rainfall accompanied by temporary gusty winds across the country. Maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla, and Payra remain under Local Cautionary Signal No. 3. Hydrological conditions have improved significantly since the peak of the emergency. As of 16 July, only the Kushiyara River remained above the danger level at two monitoring stations, Markuli in Sunamganj and Fenchuganj in Sylhet. Water levels along the Surma River and other major rivers in the north-eastern region have continued to recede, and flood conditions in low-lying areas of Sylhet and Sunamganj are expected to improve further. Similarly, water levels in the Teesta, Dharla, and Dudhkumar rivers in Rangpur Division have fallen and are projected to continue decreasing. Nevertheless, localized flooding, waterlogging, and landslide risks persist in several areas where saturated soils, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to affect communities. The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) Emergency Operations Centre remains active and continues to monitor the evolving situation. At the peak of the emergency, flood conditions deteriorated rapidly. Several rivers, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu, and Khowai, exceeded danger levels, with the Sangu River in Bandarban rising more than two metres above its danger threshold. Rising river levels threatened low-lying communities in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh, and the northern river basins, causing widespread disruption to livelihoods, infrastructure, transportation networks, and basic services. The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,116,174 people have been affected across 10 districts . The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people were temporarily displaced , while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters were opened to accommodate affected populations. Government reporting further indicates that 267,918 households were stranded or isolated by floodwaters across seven districts. Media reports citing MoDMR indicate that at least 59 people lost their lives nationwide as a result of floods and landslides. Housing damage has been extensive across the affected areas. Preliminary government assessments indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban , 13,860 in Chattogram , 1,040 in Khagrachhari , 1,613 in Cox’s Bazar . However, the full extent of housing damage remains unclear as standing water, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to hamper detailed assessments. According to the MoDMR situation update on 18 July 2026, a total of 374 unions and four municipalities across 56 upazilas have been affected by the ongoing floods. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems have been severely disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts . In many areas, water supply infrastructure remains submerged, damaged, or contaminated by floodwaters carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste, and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 water points had been fully or partially damaged, increasing risks of waterborne disease outbreaks and reducing access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities. The floods have also caused substantial damage to agriculture, livestock, and fisheries, threatening household incomes, food security, and rural livelihoods. According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), approximately 54,470 hectares of cropland and 324,358 farming households have been affected by heavy rainfall and associated hazards. Crop losses alone are estimated at more than 54,409 hectares of agricultural land . The fisheries sector has sustained particularly severe damage, with preliminary assessments from the Department of Fisheries (DoF) indicating losses of 7,613 metric tons of fish and prawns . Floodwaters washed away 21,764 fishponds and 784 commercial enclosures covering 8,966 hectares , resulting in estimated losses of approximately USD 18.3 million . The livestock sector has also been heavily impacted. Approximately 266,038 cattle and buffalo , 173,592 goats and sheep , 2.85 million chickens , and 62,811 ducks have been affected. Reported animal deaths include 62 cattle , 139 goats , 59 sheep , 154,528 chickens , and 2,063 ducks . Total losses in the livestock sector are estimated at BDT 576.2 million (approximately USD 4.7 million) . Combined losses across the fisheries and livestock sectors are estimated at approximately USD 23 million . The most severely affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj , where communities continue to face challenges related to damaged housing, disrupted livelihoods, limited access to essential services, and deteriorated infrastructure. In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and surrounding host communities. Across the 33 refugee camps, flooding and landslides affected more than 28,000 people , damaged over 3,100 shelters , and displaced more than 4,700 individuals . Multiple casualties and injuries were reported as a result of landslides and flood-related incidents. UNHCR has confirmed 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees , while thousands of people have been left homeless following landslides and shelter collapses, further increasing humanitarian needs among already vulnerable populations. The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has maintained a coordinated multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected communities. Response measures have included the opening of more than 1,000 evacuation shelters , the distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water, and other relief items, as well as the deployment of the Bangladesh Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and Civil Defence, and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation, and relief operations. The Government has also mobilised 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas to address urgent health needs and reduce public health risks. In addition, the Government has allocated 3,350 metric tons of rice , BDT 23.5 million in cash assistance , and 4,200 bundles of corrugated galvanized iron (CGI) sheets alongside BDT 12.6 million for shelter repair and reconstruction support for affected households across seven districts. National and district-level coordination mechanisms remain active to monitor the evolving situation, facilitate early warning dissemination, support affected communities, and prioritize assistance to the hardest-hit areas. Efforts are ongoing to restore essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian and early recovery needs as floodwaters continue to recede.
actions: The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) activated its Central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) immediately following the onset of the flood emergency and continues to coordinate response efforts across flood- and landslide-affected districts in south-eastern and north-eastern Bangladesh. The EOC remains operational to facilitate real-time information management, situation monitoring, and coordination with district units, government authorities, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Participating National Societies (PNSs), and other humanitarian partners, ensuring a timely, coordinated, and effective response. To support immediate response operations, BDRCS has mobilized emergency resources through its contingency funds and partner contributions. A total of BDT 2.6 million has been released to district units in Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj to facilitate rapid response activities and assist affected communities. To strengthen evacuation, rescue, and emergency response capacities, BDRCS deployed a wide range of rescue equipment and emergency supplies, including 12 rubber rescue boats, 110 life jackets, 135 rescue helmets, 135 rescue boots, 145 pairs of rescue gloves, five generators, and 5,500 jerrycans, together with rescue ropes, rope bags, float plates, and rescue panels. These assets have enhanced the operational effectiveness of district units and volunteers engaged in life-saving interventions in affected communities. BDRCS has provided emergency food assistance to 6,450 flood-affected households across Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj. Distributed food packages included rice, puffed rice, lentils, edible oil, salt, sugar, biscuits, oral rehydration salts (ORS), soap, sanitary pads, safe drinking water, and other essential household items. These interventions have helped address immediate food security and basic needs among affected populations. To respond to critical health and WASH needs, BDRCS deployed four Mobile Water Treatment Units (MWTUs) and distributed more than 5,114 litres of safe drinking water to affected communities in Bandarban and Chattogram districts. In addition, two emergency mobile medical teams were deployed with essential medicines and relief supplies to provide primary healthcare services and support disease prevention efforts in flood-affected areas. In Cox’s Bazar, BDRCS continues to respond through its Population Movement Operation (PMO), supporting both Rohingya refugees and host communities affected by flooding and landslides. Response activities include early warning dissemination, emergency relocation support, search and rescue operations, and coordination through Camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs) and humanitarian partners across all 33 refugee camps. PMO teams have provided emergency shelter assistance to 494 affected households in Camps 11 and 12, while WASH volunteers continue to assess damaged facilities and coordinate rehabilitation efforts with sector partners. Health teams remain engaged in community outreach, referrals, household visits, and the provision of essential health services, including outpatient and maternal healthcare. Through its extensive volunteer network and field teams, BDRCS continues to address the urgent needs of flood- and landslide-affected refugees and host communities. Recognizing the scale of the emergency, BDRCS formally requested IFRC support on 8 July 2026 to launch a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation for flood- and landslide-affected populations in the Rohingya camps and adjacent host communities in Cox’s Bazar. In response, IFRC approved and launched a CHF 475,000 DREF operation to support life-saving interventions, including early warning dissemination, evacuation support, search and rescue, emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, cash and voucher assistance (CVA), volunteer mobilization, and operational coordination. The DREF operation complements ongoing efforts by BDRCS, government authorities, and humanitarian partners while strengthening support to the most vulnerable communities. To strengthen Red Cross Red Crescent Movement coordination and review the evolving humanitarian situation, BDRCS convened an emergency coordination meeting on 16 July with IFRC, ICRC, and in-country Participating National Societies (PNSs). The meeting provided updates on the flood situation, damage assessments, response achievements, and operational challenges across affected districts. Given the continued deterioration in humanitarian conditions, extensive damage, emerging needs, and the expansion of affected areas beyond the initial operational scope, BDRCS has developed an enhanced response plan aimed at scaling up humanitarian assistance for the most vulnerable and severely affected households. Planned interventions include the mobilization of additional food parcels, mobile water treatment plants, emergency medical teams, essential household items, cash assistance, and agricultural recovery support. In light of increasing humanitarian needs and widening response gaps, BDRCS has requested IFRC to consider expanding the current DREF operation and has appealed to Participating National Societies to mobilize additional international resources to support a larger-scale response and early recovery effort across the flood-affected districts.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Severe storms

title: Heavy rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam
summary: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Heavy rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #2 (2026-07-19)
description: Heavy rainfall from 15–17 July triggered flash floods and landslides across Lai Chau Province, with Muong Than Commune being the worst affected. In response to the severity of the disaster, the Lai Chau Provincial People's Committee declared a state of disaster emergency for Muong Than on 17 July (Decision No. 1501/QĐ-UBND). Initial reports indicate that flash floods destroyed and buried houses in several villages, including Doi 9, Doi 11, Sap Ngua, Che Bo and Chit. National Highways 32 and 279, together with several local roads, have been cut off by landslides, significantly disrupting access and emergency response. Casualty figures continue to be updated as search and rescue operations progress. As of the morning of 18 July, authorities reported at least four fatalities, four people missing and seven injured, while approximately 80 households (358 people) have been evacuated from high-risk areas. According to the initial rapid reports from Lao Cai, Lai Chau, Dien Bien and Son La provinces, heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides occurring between 15 and 17 July 2026 caused the following impacts: Human impact: Four person was killed, four people remain missing/unaccounted for, and seven people were injured (all in Lai Chau Province). Housing: A total of 20 houses were destroyed (17 in Lai Chau and 3 in Son La); 113 houses were damaged (88 in Lao Cai, 2 in Lai Chau, 13 in Dien Bien and 10 in Son La); 42 households were urgently evacuated (26 in Lai Chau and 16 in Son La); and 46 houses were affected by flooding and landslides (29 in Lai Chau and 17 in Dien Bien). Agriculture: Approximately 238.82 hectares of rice and other crops were damaged, including 65.51 ha in Lao Cai, 101.44 ha in Lai Chau, 31.67 ha in Dien Bien, and 40.2 ha in Son La . Livestock: 25 livestock animals and 45 poultry were lost. Transport: Multiple landslides caused significant disruption to transportation. In Lai Chau, several sections of National Highways 4H, 12, 32 and 279 , as well as Provincial Roads 127, 128, 129, 133, 133B, 134 and 135 , were blocked. In Son La, 32 landslide sites were recorded along Provincial Road 109. In Dien Bien, disruptions occurred on National Highways 12 and 279 and Provincial Road 143 , while numerous commune and village roads across the affected provinces were also blocked. Power supply: In Lai Chau Province, approximately 1,373 electricity customers remained without power. Total estimated losses to housing, crops, vegetation, roads and power lines amount to more than VNĐ120 billion (US$4.6 million).
actions: The Viet Nam Red Cross (VNRC) has mobilized its provincial chapter, district branches and volunteers to support the ongoing emergency response in Lai Chau Province. In coordination with local authorities, Red Cross volunteers are providing logistical support by preparing and delivering food, drinking water and refreshments for military personnel and emergency responders conducting search and rescue operations. Simultaneously, the VNRC is carrying out rapid assessments of humanitarian needs and maintaining close coordination with local authorities to determine appropriate assistance for affected communities as the situation evolves.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Ouneine-Ijoukak Wildfire
summary: MAR: Fire - 07-2026 - Ouneine-Ijoukak Wildfire
description: On Wednesday, July 15, a wildfire has broken out in the forest area located between the mountainous communes of Ounaine, in Taroudant Province, and Ijoukak, in Al Haouz province, west-central and southwestern Morocco. The fire spread rapidly due to a combination of strong winds, high temperatures, and rugged mountainous terrain, increasing the risk to surrounding forest ecosystems and nearby communities. Early estimates indicated an affected area of 100 hectares. Emergency response operations were swiftly launched to contain the blaze. Access to the affected area is challenging because of the steep and difficult terrain, limiting the deployment of heavy firefighting equipment and complicating suppression efforts. Intervention focused on preventing the fire from reaching nearby inhabited areas through manual extinction and aerial firefighting. According to the latest official statements, 14 hectares have been consumed by the fires in Al Haouz. Authorities in Taroudant are yet to release corresponding figures. While the fire is reportedly contained on the Ijoukak side with no deaths or injuries, authorities remain vigilant. MRCS continues to assess the situation in coordination with the local actors.
actions: Monitoring the situation

title: Heavy Rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam
summary: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Heavy Rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam
description: Persistent heavy rainfall continues to affect northern Viet Nam, particularly the northwestern mountainous provinces, increasing the risk of flash floods, landslides and localised flooding. According to the Viet Nam Disaster and Dyke Management Authority (VDDMA), rainfall recorded between 19:00 on 16 July and 08:00 on 17 July reached exceptionally high levels in several locations, including 240 mm in Chế Tạo (Lào Cai Province), 224.4 mm in Nậm Păm (Sơn La Province) and 126.6 mm in Tà Mít (Lai Châu Province). National authorities remain on high alert as saturated ground conditions and continued rainfall increase the likelihood of rapid-onset disasters in vulnerable communities. According to rapid reports from the Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Lào Cai, Lai Châu and Điện Biên provinces, heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and strong winds between the evening of 15 July and 16 July caused localised damage to housing, agriculture and transport infrastructure. A total of nine houses were affected by flooding and landslides, while 34.5 hectares of rice fields were damaged and 10 head of livestock were swept away in Lào Cai Province. Transportation infrastructure was also affected. Landslides disrupted traffic at four locations along National Highways 12, 32 and 279 and at 15 locations on provincial roads across Lai Châu and Điện Biên provinces. A major landslide completely washed away the roadbed at Km76+250 on National Highway 12 in Lai Châu Province, with restoration expected to take approximately two days. At the time of reporting, no large-scale humanitarian emergency has been reported at the national level. However, weather forecasts indicate that heavy rainfall is expected to continue over the coming days, maintaining the risk of flash floods, landslides and localized flooding, particularly in remote mountainous areas.
actions: The Viet Nam Red Cross (VNRC) continues to coordinate closely with national and provincial disaster management authorities to monitor the evolving situation. Provincial Red Cross chapters in high-risk northern provinces remain on standby to conduct rapid needs assessments and provide emergency assistance should humanitarian needs arise, or the situation deteriorate.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Flooding and landslide caused by Typhoon Maysak
summary: LAO: Flood - 06-2026 - Flooding and landslide caused by Typhoon Maysak #3 (2026-07-08)
description: Following the widespread flooding reported across several provinces after Typhoon Maysak's passage, heavy and persistent rainfall continued to affect parts of the Lao PDR on 7–8 July 2026. According to the latest forecast from the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH), unstable weather conditions are expected to persist across multiple provinces, with rainfall probabilities ranging from approximately 25 to 65 per cent. Areas with higher rainfall probabilities remain at risk of continued flooding, flash floods and localised landslides. As of 7–8 July 2026, flooding has significantly affected Kounkham and Nakai districts in Khammouane Province in central Lao PDR. Rising water levels have inundated residential areas, agricultural land and key transportation routes. The Kounkham–Kong Lor road section between Nakham and Nakang villages has been submerged and is impassable to all vehicles. Floodwaters have entered houses in Nakang, Kaeng, and Muang Namsang villages, while agricultural land and rice fields have also been inundated, threatening livelihoods and food production. Flooding has also isolated several communities. Road access to Nong Hang Kao village has been completely cut off. In Natan village, Nakai District, water levels continued to rise on 8 July, reaching levels close to the second floors of residential houses in several locations. Residents have begun relocating livestock and valuable household belongings to safer areas using motorized boats as floodwaters continue to rise. In addition to flooding, a landslide occurred on the morning of 8 July along National Road 8A between Phou Pha Man and Khoun Ngeun villages in Kounkham District, temporarily blocking traffic and further disrupting transportation. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely as rainfall is forecast to continue, increasing the risk of additional flooding and landslides. At the time of reporting, no casualties have been officially reported, while damage assessments remain ongoing.
actions: Lao Red Cross (LRC) continues to closely monitor the evolving flood situation in Khammouane Province through its headquarters and provincial branches, maintaining coordination with provincial and district authorities, disaster management committees and other relevant stakeholders. The National Society is conducting continuous monitoring and assessments of affected communities, identifying emerging humanitarian needs and monitoring access constraints caused by flooding and landslides. LRC remains prepared to support evacuation efforts, relief distributions and other emergency response activities should conditions deteriorate. The National Society is also disseminating safety information and public awareness messages to vulnerable communities in flood-prone areas.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Dengue Out break Sri Lanka
summary: LKA: Epidemic - 07-2026 - Dengue Out break Sri Lanka #2 (2026-07-16)
description: The signs of escalation set out in BEACON's report on 03 Jul 2026 have now been met: high-risk MOH divisions have expanded beyond 124 (now 175); the case fatality rate (CFR) has risen above the 0.05% historical baseline (now 0.07%); and case counts have not declined in July. The timing is the central concern. The southwest monsoon peak was expected to wane by mid-July, yet week 27 produced the highest weekly total of the year, with 44 newly designated high-risk areas. An epidemic curve that continues to accelerate as its principal seasonal driver recedes indicates that transmission is being sustained by factors that will not resolve with the rainfall and that the curve has not yet reached its apex. Gampaha's displacement of Colombo as the leading district is analytically significant rather than incidental. Gampaha is the district with documented insecticide resistance in Aedes aegypti and Ae albopictus populations, and its emergence as the national epicenter is consistent with reduced efficacy of the fogging and adulticide components of the current response. This implies that the intensified vector-control campaign may be delivering diminishing returns precisely where the burden is now heaviest. The university clusters introduce a transmission setting that was absent in earlier phases of the outbreak. Campuses concentrate exposure in communal outdoor and shared-accommodation environments during daytime hours. Student mobility across districts creates a plausible mechanism for onward seeding, particularly if campus closures disperse cohorts to home districts. Whether school and university reopenings generate further institutional clusters is a near-term indicator to monitor. Comparative analysis and future outlook As of 10 Jul 2026, the year-to-date total of 67 143 cases has already surpassed the full-year totals of recent endemic years, including the 51 000 cases reported in 2025. At the current rate of roughly 1100 cases per day, the 100 000-case projection in BEACON's report on 23 Jun 2026 would be reached in mid-August, before the October–December northeast monsoon peak begins. On that trajectory, the 2019 epidemic (105 049 reported cases) is no longer a distant comparator but a plausible outcome of the current monsoon season alone. The critical determinant of the 2026 total is therefore not the current peak but the August–September inter-monsoon trough. Sri Lanka has historically seen incidence decline between the two monsoon peaks; if that decline does not occur, the country will enter the northeast monsoon season with a saturated hospital system, an expanded high-risk geography, and a partially immune population exposed to a dominant serotype.
actions: SLRCS is planning to revise the ongoing DREF appeal as per the request made by the National Dengue Control Unit.

summary: LAO: Flood - 07-2026 - Flooding as a result of Typhoon Maysak #4 (2026-07-14)
description: Following Typhoon Maysak, which brought several days of moderate-to-heavy rainfall beginning on 2 July 2026, widespread flooding affected multiple parts of the Lao PDR. The combined effects of flash floods, river flooding, landslides and prolonged inundation caused significant damage to housing, agriculture, transportation infrastructure, livelihoods, and other community assets across Luang Namtha, Bokeo, Phongsali, Vientiane, Bolikhamxai, Khammouane, and Savannakhet provinces. According to the Lao National Disaster Management Committee (NDMC), four provinces, five districts and 28 villages were affected. A total of 3,822 households, representing approximately 21,067 people, including 8,217 women, were impacted by the flooding. Khammouane Province was among the worst-affected areas, particularly Nakai and Koun Kham districts, where flooding resulted in evacuations, damage to residential areas and agricultural land, and disruption to transportation and essential services. In Koun Kham District, 14 households were evacuated to temporary shelters, while additional stranded travellers were accommodated by local authorities. Although floodwaters have begun to recede in some areas, damage assessments remain ongoing. Government authorities and humanitarian partners continue to monitor the situation and identify priority recovery needs, including food assistance, safe drinking water, agricultural inputs and support for vulnerable households.
actions: The Lao Red Cross (LRC) National Headquarters has instructed its Disaster Management Office and provincial branches to closely monitor the evolving situation and coordinate with disaster management committees at all levels to support affected communities. Provincial and district Red Cross branches have conducted rapid assessments, coordinated with local authorities to identify humanitarian needs and regularly reported updates to the National Headquarters. In Khammouane Province, the Provincial Red Cross and Nakai District Red Cross installed an AP700 water treatment unit in Na Hang Village on 8 July 2026 to provide safe drinking water to flood-affected communities. LRC is continuing detailed assessments to identify households with significant losses and plans to provide cash-based assistance during the recovery phase based on assessment findings. Many of the affected villages are located within the SAFER Project, which is supported by the Swiss Red Cross (SRC). LRC is working with project partners to utilize available emergency response resources, conduct detailed needs assessments, and integrate recovery planning with planned Enhanced Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (EVCA) activities where appropriate.

title: Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
summary: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide
description: Bangladesh is experiencing widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across the south-eastern and north-eastern regions of the country. Although the low-pressure system that triggered the initial period of extreme rainfall has weakened and moved towards Uttar Pradesh, India, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) continues to forecast intermittent heavy to very heavy rainfall through 13 July across the divisions of Chattogram, Sylhet, Rangpur, Rajshahi, Dhaka, Khulna, and Barishal. While rainfall intensity is expected to gradually decrease in the coming days, the risk of further flooding and landslides remains elevated. Rainfall has remained exceptionally high. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf recorded 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm) and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm). Additional rainfall of 100–300 mm was forecast through 12 July, maintaining a high risk of flooding, waterlogging and landslides. Flood conditions continue to evolve. As of 11 July, several river stations remained above danger level, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu and Khowai rivers. By the evening of 11 July, seven stations on five rivers across six districts were flowing above danger level. The Sangu River in Bandarban exceeded danger level by more than two metres at its peak, while rising river levels continue to threaten low-lying areas in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh and northern river basins. The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,074,534 people have been affected across 10 districts . The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people have been temporarily displaced , while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters have been opened. Government reporting indicates that more than 267,918 households have been stranded or cut off by floodwaters across seven districts, while media reports citing the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief indicate that at least 51 people have died nationwide due to floods and landslides. Preliminary Government reports indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban and 13,860 in Chattogram . The full extent and severity of housing damage remain unclear, as standing water and access constraints continue to delay detailed assessments. Water, sanitation and hygiene ( WASH ) services have been disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts . In several areas, infrastructure remains submerged, while water sources have been damaged or contaminated by floodwater carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering ( DPHE ) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 waterpoints had been fully or partially damaged . The most affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and host communities. Across the 33 camps affected more than 28,000 people , damaged over 3,100 shelters were damaged, more than 4,700 individuals were displaced , and caused multiple fatalities and injuries associated with landslides and flooding. UNHCR has reported 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees and thousands of people left homeless following landslides and shelter collapse. The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has activated a multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected populations across the impacted districts. Emergency measures include the opening of more than 1,000 shelters, the allocation and distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water and other relief items, and the deployment of the Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation and relief operations. The Government has deployed 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas. Government authorities continue to monitor the evolving situation through national and district-level coordination mechanisms, while prioritizing assistance to the most severely affected areas, including Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Efforts are ongoing to maintain access to essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian needs in affected communities.
actions: The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) has activated its central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and is coordinating response efforts across flood- and landslide-affected districts in south-eastern and north-eastern Bangladesh. Continuous information collection, situation monitoring, and coordination with district units, government authorities, IFRC, and humanitarian partners are ongoing. BDRCS has mobilized emergency resources through a combination of internal funds and partner support. A total of BDT 1.8 million has been released to district units in Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj to support immediate response activities. To strengthen evacuation and rescue capacity, BDRCS mobilized emergency rescue equipment and non-food items including: 12 rubber boats, 110 life jackets, 135 rescue helmets, 135 rescue boots, 145 pairs of gloves, 5 generators, 5,500 jerrycans, Rescue ropes, rope bags, float plates and rescue panels. BDRCS has provided emergency food assistance to 2,220 flood-affected households across Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Food packages included rice, puffed rice, lentils, oil, salt, sugar, drinking water, biscuits, ORS, soap, sanitary pads and other essential items. In Cox's Bazar, through the Population Movement Operation (PMO), BDRCS continues to support Rohingya refugees and host communities through supporting early warning dissemination, emergency relocation, search and rescue, and coordination through Camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs) and humanitarian partners across all 33 camps. BDRCS PMO has provided emergency shelter assistance to 494 affected households in Camps 11 and 12, while WASH volunteers are assessing damaged facilities and coordinating with sector partners. Health teams continue community outreach, referrals, household visits, and essential health services, including outpatient and maternity care. Through its volunteers and field teams, BDRCS remains actively engaged in addressing the immediate needs of flood- and landslide-affected refugees and host communities, BDRCS called an emergency coordination meeting on 12 July with IFRC, ICRC and in-country Participating National Societies to update about the overall flood situation and response by BDRCS. The DREF operation is intended to complement ongoing response efforts by BDRCS and humanitarian partners while strengthening support to the most vulnerable and affected communities.

title: Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026
summary: IDN: Drought - 06-2026 - Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026 #2 (2026-07-09)
description: According to the latest seasonal outlook issued by the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics (BMKG) on 10 June 2026, Indonesia is expected to face an increased risk of drought as El Niño develops during the second half of 2026 with a moderate to strong intensity, compounded by a forecast transition of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) towards a positive phase. These climate conditions are expected to result in a longer and drier dry season across much of the country, with the peak dry season anticipated between August and September 2026. The prolonged dry conditions are likely to reduce the availability of raw water sources, increase demand for clean water distribution, affect hygiene and sanitation conditions, disrupt agricultural production, and elevate the risk of forest and land fires. Based on BMKG forecasts, lessons learned from PMI's 2023 drought operation, and coordination with PMI provincial branches, the highest-risk areas have been identified in Banten, West Java, Central Java, Special Region of Yogyakarta, East Java, Bali, West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), Lampung, and South Sulawesi. Within these ten priority provinces, PMI has identified 83 priority districts for preparedness and early response planning. The impacts of the drought are already being observed in several parts of the country. As of early July 2026, 55 districts across four provinces (West Java – 27, Central Java – 19, East Java – 8, and the Special Region of Yogyakarta – 1) have officially declared a Drought Emergency Alert Status, reflecting the increasing severity of drought conditions and the need for humanitarian assistance. Furthermore, PMI has already initiated clean water distribution operations in nine districts (five in Central Java, two in West Java, one in East Java, and one in the Special Region of Yogyakarta), demonstrating that humanitarian needs have already materialized in several locations while other priority areas remain in the preparedness phase. In response to the evolving situation, PMI has developed a national operational plan integrating Early Action, Emergency Response, and Recovery, with a primary focus on ensuring continued access to safe water for drought-affected communities. Planned interventions include community awareness campaigns on water conservation, pre-positioning of water tanker trucks and emergency WASH supplies, clean water distribution, emergency water treatment and piped water systems, as well as strengthening community capacity in water resource management and preparedness for future dry seasons. This operational focus has been determined based on the current humanitarian needs and existing national response capacities. Government health services remain functional down to the village level and are expected to continue providing essential healthcare throughout the dry season. At the same time, the Government of Indonesia has implemented a range of drought mitigation measures for the agricultural sector, including the expansion of agricultural insurance schemes, the distribution of drought-resistant rice varieties, and the promotion of climate-adaptive farming practices. PMI's intervention is therefore designed to complement government efforts by addressing the most significant humanitarian gap: ensuring access to safe water, promoting hygiene and water conservation practices, and strengthening community preparedness and resilience. Given the evolving nature of the drought and the likelihood of further geographical expansion during the peak dry season, PMI will continue to closely monitor the situation and scale up its operation based on updated forecasts, humanitarian needs, and government emergency declarations.
actions: IFRC CCD is monitoring and coordinating closely with PMI NHQ for further update from the field and for further support if required

title: Heavy Rainfall and Flooding caused by Typhoon Maysak

description: Following the heavy rainfall and flooding reported on 30 June 2026 in Bokeo and Phongsaly provinces, the weather system over the South China Sea subsequently developed into Typhoon Maysak. The storm made landfall near Quảng Ninh Province in northern Viet Nam before moving inland towards Guangxi Province, China. As of 4–5 July 2026, Maysak weakened into a tropical depression and was forecast to further dissipate into a low-pressure area over southern China. Although the storm was not expected to make landfall in the Lao PDR, its circulation, combined with a moderate-to-strong southwest monsoon, continued to generate widespread rainfall across the country. According to the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH), strong southwest monsoon conditions continue to affect northern and central Lao PDR, bringing widespread thunderstorms and moderate to heavy rainfall. Several provinces remain at risk of flooding, flash floods and landslides, including Phongsali, Houaphanh, Bolikhamxai, Vientiane Province, Champasak, Salavan, Sekong and Attapeu. Rainfall totals of 50–80 mm within 24 hours are forecast in several areas, with isolated locations expected to receive more than 140 mm. The continued heavy rainfall has led to flooding across several provinces. Following the first major flooding event of the 2026 rainy season on 30 June, flash floods affected villages, agricultural land and infrastructure in Bokeo and Phongsaly provinces. In Phongsaly Province, floodwaters affected three villages in Bountai District, impacting 67 households (99 families, 367 people, including 177 women). The flooding damaged approximately 40 hectares of rice fields, including 5 hectares that were completely destroyed, as well as fishponds, irrigation canals, rubber plantations and a bridge. Local authorities reported that floodwaters had gradually receded and the situation had stabilized. However, detailed damage assessments remain ongoing. No fatalities or injuries have been reported. Additional weather-related incidents were reported in other parts of the country. On 4 July, floodwater washed away a wooden bridge crossing the Nam Song River near Tham Lom Cave in Vang Vieng District, Vientiane Province, following several days of continuous rainfall. On the same day, a cargo truck slid off a temporary bypass near the Houay Pasouan Bridge along Route 9 in Sepon District, Savannakhet Province, after persistent rainfall made the road conditions hazardous, causing significant traffic disruption but no reported injuries. In Thakhek District, Khammouane Province, floodwaters inundated parts of two villages following several days of heavy rainfall, compounded by inadequate drainage around Huay Pakximang. Local authorities continue to monitor the situation and assess damage. Authorities in Pakkading District, Bolikhamxay Province, have also issued a warning about the planned release of water from the Nam Theun 1 Dam spillway, beginning on 7 July, as part of reservoir management operations. Water discharge is expected to increase progressively by approximately 200 cubic metres per second each hour over an eight-hour period, reaching between 2,000 and 3,000 cubic metres per second. Water levels along the Nam Kading River are projected to rise by approximately 3–4 metres at the Phonchaloen monitoring station, potentially influenced by backwater effects from the Mekong River. Residents living downstream have been advised to remain vigilant, closely monitor official announcements, secure property and livestock, and prepare for possible flooding in low-lying areas.

The National Society maintains close coordination with the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology, provincial authorities, and local branches to monitor weather conditions and verify reports of impacts. LRC is collecting information on emerging humanitarian needs, conducting assessments where required, and remains prepared to mobilise volunteers and provide emergency relief assistance should the situation deteriorate.
