title: Zimbabwe Cholera Outbreak
summary: ZWE: Epidemic - 01-2026 - Zimbabwe Cholera Outbreak
description: The current cholera outbreak is placing increasing pressure on Zimbabwe's health system and the economy as transmission continues to expand geographically. Since the first confirmed case on 22 January 2026, the outbreak has persisted, with transmission resuming after only a 27-day interruption. The spread from the initial hotspots in Rushinga and Nyanga to five additional districts in Manicaland as well as Zvishavane in Midlands Province, has increased demand for cholera treatment services, laboratory testing, surveillance, active case finding, and risk communication. Health workers and limited public health resources are being stretched across multiple districts, increasing the risk of service disruptions and reducing the capacity to respond to concurrent health priorities. For affected communities, the outbreak has resulted in increased illness, preventable deaths, and increased vulnerability, particularly among economically active adults aged 20–40 years who account for more than half of reported cases. The concentration of cases among artisanal miners and other working-age adults in the Penhalonga mining area has disrupted livelihoods through illness, lost income, and reduced productivity, while increasing the financial burden on households seeking treatment and caring for sick family members. As the outbreak expands into new districts, more communities are exposed to health risks, fear, misinformation, and potential stigma associated with cholera. Continued transmission also increases the likelihood of wider community spread, placing additional strain on vulnerable populations with limited access to safe water, sanitation, and healthcare services. Without intensified control measures, the escalating outbreak is likely to further overwhelm local health services and deepen the socioeconomic impacts on affected households.
actions: Under the Cholera Simplified Early Action Protocol, trained Zimbabwe Red Cross volunteers were mobilised and deployed in Harare, Rushinga, Zvishavane, to conduct sanitary surveys and door-to-door RC-CATI, raising community awareness on the adoption of protective hygiene behaviours and practices to reduce cholera transmission. In Harare, volunteers also implemented bucket chlorination at water collection points to improve access to safe drinking water as part of early action. In Rushinga and Zvishavane, volunteers provided oral rehydration support to community members presenting with diarrhoeal symptoms during household visits. Currently, ZRCS is working on deploying volunteers in Mutare City and Penhalonga for door to door RC-CATI. Overall, these interventions reached approximately 124,567 people.
recommendations: Scale up vaccination campaigns and immunization coverage.; Enhance disease surveillance and laboratory testing capacities.

title: Floods

description: A catastrophic climate emergency struck Ghana's southern coastline on Monday, June 29, 2026, when torrential rains triggered devastating floods across the Greater Accra, Central, and Western regions. The relentless downpour, which began late the previous evening, completely paralyzed the Monday morning economic rush hour and submerged vast swathes of residential and commercial property. The disaster claimed at least 12 lives in the Greater Accra and prompted immediate emergency interventions as rising waters trapped hundreds of citizens in their homes and vehicles. In the Greater Accra Region, the capital city became the epicentre of the crisis, experiencing some of the highest rainfall volumes recorded in recent years (140 millimeters of rainfall). Key economic hubs and transit choke points, including the Kwame Nkrumah Circle, Kaneshie Market, Alajo, Shiashie, Madina, Abokobi, Kasoa, Weija and Adabraka, were completely inundated, forcing the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO), the Ghana Red Cross, National Fire Service and the military to deploy rescue boats to evacuate over 400 stranded residents. Compounding the chaos, a massive fire erupted at a rubber factory in Accra, stretching emergency responders to their limits as they battled flames amidst deep floodwaters. Further west along the coastal corridor, the Central Region suffered severe structural damage as raging stormwaters tore through low-lying communities. Key arterial roads connecting coastal towns were washed away or left impassable, heavily disrupting transit along the critical N1 highway corridor. The region also accounted for several of the confirmed fatalities, with local emergency services responding to multiple incidents of drowning and structural collapses caused by the intense pressure of the water. Simultaneously, the Western Region faced widespread logistical disruption as heavy, localized rain cells saturated urban and industrial zones. Secondary drainage networks failed entirely, sending torrents of water through local businesses and stalling activity around major regional shipping and trade networks. The combined impact across these three regions highlighted the vulnerability of the country's southern economic belt to sudden, extreme weather anomalies.

title: Heatwave

title: Earthquake
summary: VEN: Earthquake - 06-2026 - Earthquake
description: On 24 June 2026, two strong earthquakes, preliminarily measured at magnitudes 7.1 and 7.5, struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with epicentres near Morón, Carabobo State. The earthquakes were felt across much of the country, where the most affected areas are Capital District of Caracas and La Guaira, and less impact in Aragua and Falcon. Therefore, the national goverment of Venezuela declared the state of emergency. Preliminary information indicates damage to residential and commercial buildings, with reports of structural collapses in parts of Caracas and damage to infrastructure in several affected areas. Search and rescue operations have been activated while authorities continue rapid damage assessments. Power and telecommunications interruptions have been reported in some locations, and hospitals are receiving injured people. The full humanitarian impact is still being assessed. Official information on casualties, displaced people and infrastructure damage remains limited. Significant aftershocks are expected, posing additional risks to affected communities and emergency responders. In addition, the National Headquarters of the Venezuelan Red Cross reported critical damage in the infrastructure. Critical damage has also been reported to essential social infrastructure, including the airport and hospitals, while public services are intermittent or completely disrupted
actions: The National Society and IFRC are participating in a coordination meeting held by the Ministry of Disaster Risk Management, alongside other relief agencies present in the area to begin coordinating the response. Additionally, at the national headquarters level, the Emergency Operations Center has been activated, ambulances have been deployed in the Capital District, rescue teams have been mobilized to assist those affected by the collapse of infrastructure, and shelter facilities are being prepared for people in need of refuge. The overall situation of the emergency remains uncertain, and a preliminary assessment of the impact is expected shortly to coordinate actions following the search and rescue operations.
recommendations: Strengthen building standards and conduct structural assessments.; Establish emergency medical response teams and field hospitals.

title: Cholera outbreak in Karal health district (Hadjer Lamis province)
summary: TCD: Epidemic - 06-2026 - Cholera outbreak in Karal health district (Hadjer Lamis province)
description: The analysis of epidemiological data and field observations reveals the following elements: An epidemic still localized but at risk of spreading With 52 confirmed cases out of a total population of 124,300, the apparent overall attack rate remains low. However, this ratio is misleading: cases are concentrated in only 3 of the district's 14 areas of responsibility, meaning that the actual attack rate in the affected areas is significantly higher than the district average suggests. The lack of a population denominator specific to the affected areas is a limitation of the current analysis and should be corrected to better calibrate the response. The observed case fatality rate (≈ 1.9%) is above the threshold generally sought in a well-controlled response (usual target of less than 1%), which suggests either a delay in seeking care that is plausible in view of the fear observed around UHC2 – or inadequacies in the early management of cases, or both at the same time. High risk of geographical spread The contiguity of the Karal district with Bol via the island network, combined with the immediate proximity of an IDP site with the 3rd affected area of responsibility, places the area in a configuration with a high risk of transboundary spread and to a particularly vulnerable displaced population (density, limited access to water and sanitation, mobility). This risk should be considered a priority in response planning. A structural deficit in water, hygiene and sanitation as a driver of transmission With a non-functionality rate of water points of about 32% in urban areas and incomplete coverage outside the city, access to drinking water remains fragile. More worryingly, the lack of comprehensive mapping of sanitation facilities (latrines) prevents precise targeting of interventions, while open defecation remains widespread. This WASH deficit is likely to be the main driver of cholera transmission in the district. Problem in the continuity of care in an epidemic context The absence of staff and patients at the UHC2 could reflect an under-attendance of health centers by the population. This phenomenon, if not quickly corrected by risk communication and community engagement actions, risks leading to under-reporting of cases, delayed use of care and, ultimately, an increase in lethality and community transmission. Community coverage still partial With 14 neighbourhoods covered in urban areas and 20 villages as well as 11 other ZRs not covered by awareness-raising activities. The number of community relays mobilised (36) appears to be insufficient in view of the geographical extent of the three areas of responsibility affected. According to health officials, coverage in terms of awareness in urban areas is considered limited. It should be noted that 11 ZRs in Karal district are not yet affected. Weakened detection capabilities outside of affected areas The stock-outs of cholera RDTs in the 11 unaffected areas of responsibility are a major blind spot in the surveillance system. If cases appear in these areas, the delay in detection could jeopardize an early response and encourage an uncontrolled spread of the epidemic. In addition, the community-based epidemiological surveillance system is not effective, which could hinder the early detection and response of new cases.
actions: The CRF supported the CRT to conduct a rapid assessment of the epidemiological, clinical and environmental situation in order to prepare a coordinated emergency response plan to curb the spread of the epidemic. the FIU and the AICRL participated in the coordination meetings of the movement and the Ministry of Health.
recommendations: Scale up vaccination campaigns and immunization coverage.; Enhance disease surveillance and laboratory testing capacities.

title: MOVEMENT OF THE POPULATION OF THE DRC IN THE REPUBLIC OF CONGO
summary: COG: Population Movement - 06-2026 - MOVEMENT OF THE POPULATION OF THE DRC IN THE REPUBLIC OF CONGO
description: On 3 November 2025, a latent land dispute between the Lobalatanda and Engalango Sud communities, in the Dongo sector (Sud-Ubangi, DRC), degenerated into violence after the murder of a teacher perceived as a triggering act. The clashes left five dead, thirteen injured and burned nearly fifty houses around Tomba, forcing residents to flee. In a few days, 3,500 households (17,500 people) crossed the river to take refuge in the Republic of Congo, mainly in Bétou, Enyellé and riverside villages such as Goma, Iloko, Benga and Mouna Boli. The new arrivals, mostly women, children and the elderly, arrived without resources, with urgent needs for shelter, food, care and protection, quickly saturating the already limited local reception capacities. This violence is part of a tense historical land tenure context in South Ubangi, where rivalries over land and resources — as during the Dongo crisis in 2009 — remain recurrent in the absence of effective mediation mechanisms. They echo other land tensions in the DRC, particularly in Maï-Ndombé, where attacks by Mobondo militias in Kwamouth since 2022/2025 and the Téké–Banunu clashes in Bolobo in January 2025, which have caused the displacement of 8,957 people to the Republic of Congo, illustrate the same pattern of violent escalation around questions of legitimacy and access to land. This influx to Congo comes at a time when the country was already hosting about 70,000 refugees as of November 30, 2025, mainly in Likouala, Plateaux, Nkéni-Alima and Djoué-Léfini. The sudden arrival of more than 15,000 new displaced people is therefore increasing the pressure on a territory where resources, infrastructure and public services are already in high demand.
actions: None.
recommendations: Establish reception and assessment centers for displaced populations.; Provide emergency shelter, food, and basic healthcare services.

title: Malawi Xenophobia Population Movement Response
summary: MWI: Population Movement - 03-2026 - Malawi Xenophobia Population Movement Response
description: Between March and June, 2026, South Africans started attaching all foreigners pushing them to go out their country. This has resulted in many foreigners being chased from their settlements. This involved included beating, stealling and othe several traumatising situations. Over 9000 Malawian have since assemble at Lindera waiting centre awating to be repatriated to Malawi. Some have already been repatriated to Malawi but the majority are yet to be repatriated. The conditions there are dire with poor leaving environment, lack of food, clothing , beddings and other basic needs. The Malawi governement has offered to repatriate its citizens who have voluntarily expressed interest to do so. A reception centre has been created in Malawi where returnees are being received and helped to go to their different destinations. There are diverse needs to support the whole returning, screening and repatriation back their respective homes. This has socially and economically affected those affected as they have been disturbed, mentally torcherred, lost lovelihoods and belongings stolen. There is a huge humanitarian crisis requiring agent support
actions: Since the onset of the xenophobia crisis in South Africa, the Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS) has been at the forefront of humanitarian response, mobilizing its structures and resources to support distressed Malawians. Despite severe resource constraints, the National Society has undertaken a series of impactful activities aligned with the urgent needs of returnees: a) Activation of National Response Team: MRCS deployed its trained team to Mwanza Border Post and Kamuzu Stadium, ensuring immediate reception, screening, and support for returnees. This action provided structure and coordination at critical entry points. b) Health screening and psychosocial support: Volunteers have been conducting medical checks and delivering Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHSSP) services, addressing trauma and stress among returnees, especially women, children, and the elderly. c) Family tracing and Restoring Family Links (RFL): MRCS has facilitated communication between separated family members, helping restore connections and reduce distress among displaced individuals. d) Logistics and shelter support: The Society has deployed tents and coordinated temporary shelter arrangements at Kamuzu Stadium, mitigating overcrowding and providing basic protection against harsh weather conditions. e) Distribution of essential supplies: Food, dignity kits, bedding, and health kits have been provided where possible, though shortages remain acute. These interventions have been lifesaving, especially given the cold season and poor conditions in South African waiting centres. f) Coordination with government and partners: MRCS has worked closely with DoDMA, IOM, and other humanitarian actors to align efforts in repatriation, reception, and reintegration, ensuring a multi-sectoral response.
recommendations: Establish reception and assessment centers for displaced populations.; Provide emergency shelter, food, and basic healthcare services.

title: Floods in Moldova May-June 2026
summary: MDA: Flood - 05-2026 - Floods in Moldova May-June 2026
description: The hydrometeorological crisis that affected the Republic of Moldova from late May through mid-June 2026 caused widespread flooding and infrastructure damage across multiple regions, directly affecting an estimated up to 1,000 people. According to information from the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (GIES), the National Crisis Management Center (CNMC), and local authorities, the severe weather impacted communities in 15 districts and municipalities. The first wave of torrential rainfall and flash floods of 22 May 2026. On 23 May, the Prime Minister visited Călărași district together with the Minister of Infrastructure and Regional Development, the Minister of Internal Affairs and the Minister of Environment. The Government reported that the most affected districts were Călărași and Ungheni. In Călărași district, the Government identified Hîrjăuca and Mîndra as the most serious locations after the rupture of a protective dam. In Ungheni district, 11 localities were reported as affected. The Government also confirmed one fatality in Dereneu, Călărași district: a 48-year-old man died in circumstances associated with the heavy rains and floods recorded the previous evening. General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (GIES) interventions included pumping water, clearing fallen trees, removing dangerous objects, and conducting search-and-rescue operations. 85 specialized vehicles and more than 300 staff were deployed. It also reported temporary impacts on road and railway traffic, followed by restoration of rail movement, and partial electricity disruptions, followed by repair and reconnection works. official reporting, the torrential rains affected 25 localities across four districts: Călărași, Strășeni, Ungheni and Criuleni. The impact was concentrated at household, agricultural and local-infrastructure level. In total, 69 households were directly affected by flooding. At the same time, approximately 400 households were considered at risk of being flooded, but were protected through rapid emergency measures, including reinforcement of protective dikes, digging of drainage trenches and controlled evacuation of water. The floods also affected agricultural land and road infrastructure. Approximately 400 hectares of farmland were flooded, while around 55 km of roads were affected. According to National Crisis Management Center (CNMC), three dikes were at risk of failure within a chain of seven water-storage basins. Emergency teams worked continuously for 72 hours to reinforce these dikes using sandbags and specialized protective film. Drainage trenches were also dug to reduce water pressure. CNMC reported that, following these measures, all protective dikes had been reinforced and remained operational, preventing further flooding of localities and households that had been at risk. On 26 May 2026, the leadership of the Red Cross Society of Moldova (MRCS), together with representatives of regional branches, conducted a field mission to Călărași District to assess the humanitarian situation. The delegation visited Dereneu, Bularda, and Mândra, meeting with local authorities, affected families, social workers, and emergency responders. In Bularda, the MRCS team supported personnel engaged in reinforcing flood protection structures and later provided food supplies to emergency teams working on-site. Following the initial assessment and response, MRCS also provided humanitarian assistance to affected households. In Călărași district approximately 300 families from Bularda, Dereneu, Hîrjăuca, Mândra and Bravicea received in-kind humanitarian assistance, including hygiene products, duvets, bed linen, water filters and kitchen sets. In Bularda, where GIES teams were working continuously to consolidate the water-basin dike and prevent a larger emergency, MRCS also provided food products to personnel involved in the intervention. A second and intense wave of storms struck on 6 June 2026 The State Hydrometeorological Service had issued a Yellow Code warning for 6 June. The affected areas included Ialoveni, Strășeni, Drochia, Telenești, Soroca, Rezina, Sîngerei, Basarabeasca, Chișinău municipality and Durlești. Ialoveni district was one of the most affected areas during this episode. GIES reported impacts in Puhoi, Țipala, Gangura and Cărbuna. In Gangura commune, approximately 100 households were affected, and an approximately 8 km section of road was damaged or impacted. In Puhoi and Țipala, water accumulated massively, some households were flooded, and several local road sections were blocked. In Strășeni district, were impacted Voinova, Chirianca, Onești, Rassvet, Greblești and Strășeni municipality. Water accumulated in households and dwellings, while road sections were blocked in Chirianca and on the access road toward Voinova. In Strășeni municipality, pumping operations were conducted. Similar works were carried out in Vorniceni. Water accumulation was also reported on roadways in Recea and Căpriana. In Bucovăț, the rainfall was accompanied by hail and strong wind gusts, while in Greblești a partial electricity disconnection occurred and was later resolved. In Drochia district, slope runoff affected approximately 20 households in Gribova, including homes and cellars. IGSU and local public authorities carried out water-pumping and drainage-channel cleaning works. In Telenești district, the affected areas included Telenești municipality and Leușeni village. In Telenești municipality, a basement and a dwelling were flooded after overflow from a drainage channel. In Leușeni, water accumulation was recorded in three households. In Soroca district, a dwelling and a cellar were flooded in Bulboci village. In Rezina district, a road section in Peciște was blocked by alluvium and later cleared. In Sîngerei district, around seven gardens were flooded in Clișcăuți village, Prepelița commune; a gravel road section was damaged; and national road R6 was partially blocked. In Basarabeasca town, a fallen tree on Nicolai Gogol Street temporarily blocked traffic. In Homuteanovca, the water level was decreasing, but six households were affected, including one cellar and five agricultural plots. The Red Cross response after this episode continued to focus on household-level assistance. In Greblești, Strășeni district, SCRM reported that 11 affected families received more than 120 essential items in collaboration with the Greblești local authorities. In Cornova, Ungheni District, 5 families received 65 essential household items, including hygiene kits, bedding, water filters, and kitchen utensils such as pots and frying pans. In Călărași District, 160 families from Bularda, Dereneu, Hîrjăuca, Mândra, and Bravicea received 1,220 essential relief items, including hygiene kits, bed linen sets, blankets, water filters, water filter cartridges, pillows, and other household essentials. Additional humanitarian distributions included 330 relief items in Basarabeasca District, consisting of hygiene kits, bed linen sets, blankets, cooking pots, and water filters, as well as 96 relief items in Drochia District, where beneficiaries received assistance across eight categories, including bedding, hygiene supplies, water filters, pillows, and bed covers.The distributed items included bed linen, blankets, duvets, pillows, drinking-water filters, water-filter cartridges, tableware sets and hygiene parcels. This assistance addressed direct household needs linked to flooding, such as wet or contaminated bedding, damaged or lost domestic goods, hygiene concerns and potential safe-water needs. MRCS identified through field assessment that needs of affected households started to exceed available resources. And MRCS started to plan how to expand assistance through hygiene and cleaning kits, household goods, psychosocial support and cash assistance for families in the most vulnerable situations. The third episode took place on 11-12 June 2026. On 11 June, the State Hydrometeorological Service issued an updated warning for atmospheric instability, valid from 11 June at 15:30 until 12 June at 21:00. For Orange Code areas, the warning forecast very heavy showers with accumulated precipitation of 50-79 l/m². For Yellow Code areas, the warning forecast short-duration rains with thunderstorms, isolated heavy showers of 15-49 l/m², hail and wind gusts of up to 15-20 m/s. The main effects were water accumulation in households, basements of apartment buildings, commercial premises and public institutions; flooding of adjacent land plots; temporary blocking of vehicles; and deposits of mud and water on national and local road infrastructure. The operational impact was concentrated mainly in Telenești, Strășeni, Edineț, Ocnița, Sîngerei, Ialoveni and Drochia municipality. Telenești district recorded the highest operational impact during this episode. Water accumulation affected private households, basements of apartment buildings, commercial units and public institutions in Telenești town and Inești village. GIES carried out 19 water-evacuation interventions in Telenești district, including 16 in Telenești town and three in Inești village. These interventions targeted households, two apartment-building basements, commercial units and one public institution. Emergency teams also towed four blocked vehicles and removed one fallen tree from the carriageway. In Strășeni district, was reported significant water accumulation in Strășeni municipality and in Onești and Rădeni. In Edineț, Ocnița, Drochia and Sîngerei, the rainfall caused flooding of households, cellars, auxiliary spaces and local road sections. In Edineț district, 7 households were affected in Fetești and Trinca. There were reported mud deposits, water accumulation and temporary traffic blockages on several national and regional road sections. The State Road Administration and territorial road-maintenance units intervened in Drochia, Călărași, Ialoveni, Sîngerei, Strășeni, Cimișlia, Criuleni, Glodeni, Edineț, Briceni, Dondușeni, Nisporeni and Ocnița. There were also reported temporary electricity-distribution impacts during this episode. At distribution level, Electricity Infrastructure providers reported temporary disconnections affecting around 30,000 consumers. These incidents were mainly caused by torrential rainfall, lightning, falling branches and conductor damage. Following the repeated flood-related impacts recorded in May and June 2026, the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Republic of Moldova requested a coordination meeting to discuss the remaining needs of affected households and the potential support that could be provided by the Red Cross Society of Moldova, as the National Society. The meeting took place on 10 June 2026 and was attended by Executive Director of the Red Cross Society of Moldova and representative of International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. During the meeting, the Ministry highlighted that community social workers, local competent institutions and humanitarian partners had been mobilized in the affected communities from the first days after the floods. Social workers conducted household visits, assessed the situation of affected families and helped direct assistance toward people who could not be displaced or who had limited capacity to access support independently. Discussion confirmed that some needs remained uncovered, particularly among households whose homes, bedding, hygiene conditions, household items or recovery capacity had been directly affected by flooding. Following this coordination discussion, the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection sent an official request to the Red Cross Society of Moldova to support affected households and vulnerable beneficiaries whose needs had not yet been fully addressed. The request provides an institutional basis for further Red Cross engagement in close coordination with social assistance structures, local public authorities and other competent institutions. According to preliminary information collected to date, approximately 390 households, representing approximately 1,093 people, including children, were directly affected by these events. Quantified immediate needs for 1,093 people: 1. Drinking water – 16,500 liters/day for 21 days to prevent dehydration and water-borne diseases 2. Basic food products – food packages for 21 days 3. Personal and household hygiene products – 1,093 sets to reduce the risk of infections in collective shelters 4. Bed linen and blankets – 300 sets of duvets/pillows/sheets. Nighttime temperatures of 8-10°C maintain the risk of hypothermia in the elderly 5. Clothing and footwear – for all age groups, considering the loss of household goods The floods severely affected localities in the districts of Călărași, Strășeni, Criuleni, Ialoveni, Nisporeni, Drochia, Soroca, Telenești, Orhei, Edineț, Ocnița, Dondușeni, Ungheni, Basarabeasca, Căușeni, Anenii Noi and Cimișlia, as well as the municipality of Bălți. The situation was aggravated by the repetitive nature of the meteorological phenomena, with several districts being successively affected by waves of precipitation and flooding in a relatively short period of time. These repeated events reduced the recovery capacity of the affected households, amplified the vulnerability of the population and generated cumulative effects on communities already affected by previous episodes. Repeated hydrometeorological events have put considerable pressure on the capacity of central and local public institutions to respond effectively and in a timely manner to the needs of the affected population. Available human, logistical and financial resources have been repeatedly mobilized to assess the damage, provide emergency assistance and support to affected households. Despite the efforts of the public authorities and the Moldovan Red Cross Society, the scale and costs of the damage exceed the current capacity to respond and support affected households at the national level. The assessments carried out indicate the existence of significant humanitarian needs that cannot be fully covered by the currently available resources, and the existing capacities are insufficient to respond in a timely manner to all the needs identified in the affected communities. Some of the affected households continue to face precarious living conditions, including partially or completely uninhabitable housing, damage to essential goods and limited access to basic services. In particular, for families with children, the elderly, people with disabilities and other vulnerable groups, the situation remains difficult, and the current conditions pose significant risks to their health, safety and well-being. Preliminary data indicate that a significant proportion of affected households belong to vulnerable groups, including families with young children, elderly people living alone and people with disabilities. In the absence of adequate access to drinking water, hygiene products and adequate housing conditions, there are increased risks to the health of the affected population. The analysis of needs reported by the authorities and territorial structures highlights the existence of priority needs related to access to drinking water, basic food products, personal and household hygiene items, bed linen, blankets, clothing, footwear and other essential goods necessary to restore minimum living conditions for affected households. In response to the remaining unmet needs, the Red Cross Society of Moldova is considering the submission of a request for support through the IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund. The proposed response is expected to include a cash assistance component as the main modality to help vulnerable flood-affected households cover priority needs that remain unaddressed after the initial in-kind assistance and local response measures.
actions: Since the onset of the floods, the Red Cross Society of Moldova has carried out rapid damage and needs assessments in close coordination with local authorities and emergency services, identifying the most affected communities and vulnerable households. The National Society has provided humanitarian assistance to 176 families across the districts of Călărași, Strășeni, Ungheni, Basarabeasca, and Drochia, distributing essential relief items such as hygiene kits, bedding, blankets, water filters, kitchenware, and other household supplies. In parallel, the Red Cross supported frontline emergency responders with food assistance during flood protection operations and continues to monitor affected communities, assess evolving needs, and prepare for further relief and psychosocial support interventions as resources allow.
recommendations: Strengthen early warning systems and evacuation procedures for flood-prone areas.; Enhance drainage infrastructure and water management systems.

title: Central Sulawesi Earthquake – Magnitude 6.7
summary: IDN: Earthquake - 06-2026 - Central Sulawesi Earthquake – Magnitude 6.7
description: On 16 June 2026 at 10:27 WIB, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck Central Sulawesi Province at a depth of 10 km. The epicentre was located approximately 42 km southeast of Palu City. The earthquake was strongly felt in Palu (MMI VI–VII) and Sigi (MMI V–VI). At the same time, light-to-moderate tremors were reported across several districts in Sulawesi, Gorontalo, and East Kalimantan. No tsunami warning was issued. According to preliminary assessments by local authorities and PMI, the earthquake affected Palu City, Sigi District, Parigi Moutong District, and Poso District. A total of 5,744 people (1,436 households) have been affected, including one death, three people seriously injured, and 71 people with minor injuries. In Sigi District alone, 5,694 people were affected across five sub-districts. Damage assessments reported 30 houses destroyed, 110 houses moderately damaged, and 1,350 houses slightly damaged. Public infrastructure was also affected, including schools, places of worship, government buildings, a health centre, bridges, water supply systems, and road access. As of 17 June 2026, BMKG had recorded 466 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 3.8 to 5.2. While electricity and telecommunications services have largely been restored and daily activities have resumed, access to some affected communities remains constrained due to landslides, damaged bridges, and disrupted road networks. Assessments are ongoing and figures may change as additional information becomes available.
actions: The Indonesian Red Cross (PMI) Central Sulawesi Chapter has mobilized 11 personnel, including staff and volunteers, to support the response operation. Activities undertaken include rapid assessments and field data collection, evacuation support, ambulance standby services, first aid assistance for affected people, and coordination with local authorities and emergency response agencies. PMI continues to monitor the situation and update impact information as assessments progress.
recommendations: Strengthen building standards and conduct structural assessments.; Establish emergency medical response teams and field hospitals.

title: Severe storm and strong winds
summary: SVN: Other - 10-2026 - Severe storm and strong winds
description: Storms between 10 and 11 June 2026 caused extensive damage to residential and agricultural buildings, transport infrastructure, and agricultural land across several parts of Slovenia. The highest number of damaged structures was recorded in the Municipality of Komenda, where more than 150 buildings were affected. According to initial assessments, there was hardly a house in the most severely affected areas that did not sustain some form of damage. title: Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) in Iraq/IRCS
summary: IRQ: Epidemic - 05-2026 - Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) in Iraq/IRCS
description: Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) remains a significant public health concern in Iraq during the 2026 seasonal transmission period. The disease, which is endemic in the country, is primarily associated with exposure to infected ticks, direct contact with infected livestock, and handling of contaminated animal blood and tissues during slaughtering and meat processing activities. Iraq continues to experience seasonal increases in CCHF cases during late spring and early summer, corresponding with heightened livestock movement, agricultural activities, and increased human-animal interaction. According to official reports from the Iraqi Ministry of Health and publicly available surveillance updates, Iraq recorded a continued rise in confirmed CCHF cases during May 2026. By 24 May 2026, reported infections and associated fatalities had been documented across multiple governorates, confirming ongoing transmission and reinforcing concerns regarding the expansion of disease activity during the peak transmission season. Thiqar Governorate emerged as the most affected area, accounting for the highest number of reported cases nationwide, while additional infections were reported in other southern and central governorates, including Diyala, Kirkuk, Basra, Maysan, Wasit, and Baghdad. The epidemiological situation observed in 2026 reflects patterns documented in previous years, where the highest burden of disease occurs between May and July. Historical surveillance data from Iraq indicate that southern governorates consistently experience the greatest impact due to a combination of livestock density, agricultural livelihoods, informal slaughtering practices, and environmental conditions favourable to tick proliferation. High-risk population groups continue to include livestock breeders, butchers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers, animal traders, and rural households engaged in animal husbandry. During coordination meetings held between the Iraqi Red Crescent Society, the Ministry of Health, Veterinary Directorates, and Governorate Health Directorates, stakeholders highlighted the need for strengthened surveillance, community awareness, risk communication, and integrated One Health interventions to mitigate further transmission. Discussions emphasized the importance of coordinated action between public health and veterinary authorities to improve early detection, enhance infection prevention measures, and reduce community exposure to identified risk factors. The current situation is further compounded by the approaching Ashura commemorations, one of the largest annual mass gatherings in Iraq, expected to attract millions of pilgrims to Karbala and other religious centres, including Najaf, Baghdad, Babil, Wasit, Maysan, thiqar, and Basra. Increased population movement, temporary food preparation sites, informal slaughtering activities, and heightened demand for livestock products may elevate the risk of exposure to infected animals and contaminated materials. While CCHF is not primarily transmitted through casual human contact, the scale of population movement and associated animal handling practices could increase opportunities for disease spread and place additional pressure on local health systems. Given the ongoing transmission reported during May 2026, the concentration of cases in high-risk governorates, and the anticipated influx of pilgrims during the Ashura period, there is a critical need for enhanced preparedness and response measures. Priority actions include intensified surveillance, strengthened community engagement, expanded public awareness campaigns, enforcement of safe slaughtering practices, improved tick-control interventions, and continued coordination among the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Agriculture, Veterinary Services, local authorities, humanitarian partners, and the Iraqi Red Crescent Society. Given the evolving epidemiological situation and the anticipated increase in population movement during upcoming religious events, immediate and coordinated preparedness and response actions are required to mitigate public health risks and support affected communities.
actions: Iraqi Red Crescent Response to CCHF In response to the increased risk of Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF), the Iraqi Red Crescent Society (IRCS), in close coordination with the Ministry of Health, local health directorates, veterinary authorities, and community stakeholders, implemented a comprehensive prevention and awareness campaign across 10 high-risk governorates. The intervention focused on villages, peri-urban communities, livestock markets, butcher shops, and other public gathering areas where exposure to infection is more likely. Through community engagement activities, risk communication, and health awareness sessions, IRCS volunteers disseminated key prevention messages on safe livestock handling, personal protective measures, early recognition of symptoms, and timely healthcare seeking. procedures. • Activate and reinforce rapid response teams to support timely outbreak investigation and field verification. • Intensify preparedness planning ahead of Ashura mass gatherings, including contingency planning and surge capacity measures. • Expand tick-control interventions and strengthen livestock health campaigns in coordination with relevant authorities. • Increase inspection and monitoring of livestock movement between governorates to reduce cross-regional transmission risks. • Conduct targeted awareness and risk communication activities for livestock owners, butchers, and at-risk occupational groups. • Deploy volunteers to support community-level awareness campaigns, particularly in rural and peri-urban areas. • Deliver structured risk communication sessions to improve community understanding of prevention measures and early care seeking. • Support dissemination of preventive messaging during high-risk periods, including Ashura-related gatherings. • Engage community influencers, including religious leaders and market associations, to enhance outreach effectiveness. • Strengthen referral pathways and community-based reporting mechanisms to improve case identification and notification. • Establish governorate-level coordination mechanisms to ensure multi-sectoral alignment and operational coherence. • Conduct regular information sharing among operational actors to support real-time situational awareness. • Develop and disseminate unified risk communication messages to ensure consistency across all stakeholders. • Implement joint field monitoring and assessment visits in identified hotspot areas to guide evidence-based interventions. • Enhance multi-sectoral preparedness measures ahead of peak pilgrimage and mass gathering periods.

title: Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026
summary: IDN: Drought - 06-2026 - Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026
description: Indonesia is forecasted to experience prolonged dry conditions during the 2026 dry season due to the combined influence of El Niño conditions and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). According to BMKG, the dry season is expected to begin earlier than normal in many regions, with 57.2% of seasonal zones (ZOM) predicted to experience a longer dry season and 64.5% of Indonesia forecasted to receive below-normal rainfall accumulation during the June–September period. The provinces considered most at risk include Central Java, East Java, DI Yogyakarta, West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), West Java, Banten, South Sulawesi, Lampung, Bali, and parts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi. Forecasts indicate a high probability of very low rainfall (<50 mm/month) across these regions between June and October 2026, increasing the likelihood of water shortages, crop failure, reduced agricultural productivity, public health concerns, and increased risk of forest and land fires. Historical operational data from PMI’s drought response in 2023 showed significant humanitarian impacts, including prolonged clean water distribution operations across 131 districts/cities in 21 provinces with more than 93 million litres of water distributed. Provinces such as Central Java, East Java, NTB, and DI Yogyakarta recorded the highest operational demand, indicating high exposure and recurring vulnerability to drought conditions. The projected impacts for 2026 include: o Reduced access to safe water for domestic use and sanitation; o Increased reliance on water trucking and emergency water supply systems; o Livelihood disruption, particularly among rain-fed farming communities; o Increased heat-related illnesses and water-borne disease risks due to limited clean water access; o Potential worsening of forest and land fire risks in parts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi; o Increased economic pressure on vulnerable households due to rising water and food costs. The most vulnerable groups include low-income households, rural farming communities, women-headed households, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, and communities living in drought-prone and water-scarce areas. Coastal communities in some areas may also experience saline water intrusion as river discharge decreases during prolonged dry periods.
actions: Early Actions Taken by National Society (PMI) A. Emergency Response Phase • Water Supply: Large-scale clean water distribution (water trucking). • Health Services: o Operation of Smoke-Free Houses (Safe Houses) in West and Central Kalimantan. o Mobile health services and continued Community-Based Surveillance (CBS). • Multi-Purpose Cash Grants (MPCG): Prioritized for livelihood protection (mitigation for crop failure/agricultural loss) and household water purchasing. • Community Engagement: Strengthening CEA and PGI protocols during response. • Support Services: NSD (operational support, insurance, lessons learned workshops), and sectoral Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM). title: Farmers-herders conflict
summary: TCD: Population Movement - 06-2026 - Farmers-herders conflict
description: Sequence of incidents: On June 4, 2026, in the village of Selh, a farmer was working in her cereal field when a herd led by Fulani women herders (Foulbé) entered the plot. An altercation turned into a fight, during which the farmer was hit in the forehead with a hammer. Alerted, the farmers sued the herders and killed two people in retaliation. The injured in this altercation were transferred to Bongor Hospital for intensive care. On the night of June 4, clashes continued in the two communities causing 04 deaths, two on each side (farmers and herders) and on the evening of 05, Fulani nomads armed with arrows and firearms attacked several surrounding villages (Kouroup village, Batenor and Kolté), burning houses, granaries and essential goods, and killing several inhabitants. The attackers were using motorcycles to escape quickly after their attacks. In total, 3 villages directly affected (Kouroup, Batenor, Kolté) suffered massive destruction: houses burned, granaries burned, mills and motorcycles burned, and household items destroyed. Travel and reception of victims: On 6 June 2026, a joint mission of the Red Cross Society of Chad (CRT), with the support of the International Federation (IFRC), was deployed to the field to assess the situation. This mission noted the presence of hundreds of displaced people, grouped in particular in the health centres of Zigui Marba and Holom, which have been converted into reception sites. The majority of the displaced are women and children, who are severely affected psychologically. According to local authorities, including the sub-prefect and the village chief of Kouroup, at least ten villages have been affected, resulting in the displacement of more than 1,000 households. Displaced populations have taken refuge in churches, health centres or with host families. The injured people were evacuated to the health facilities of Koyom, Djoumane and Bongor. It should be noted that the village of Zigui Marba, although not directly affected, hosts a large number of displaced people. Reception conditions are particularly precarious, characterized by a lack of food, medicine, shelter and health infrastructure. The head of the health center said he did not have the necessary resources to ensure adequate emergency care. Testimonials and safety measures During the field mission to Kouroup, identified as one of the most affected villages, consultations were conducted with the sub-prefect of Kim, local authorities and community representatives. These exchanges confirmed that the violence had affected at least ten villages, including Kouroup, Koldé, Samasson, Koyon, Molom, Dereb, Selh 1, Selh 2 and Zigui Marba. The displaced population is mainly composed of women, children and the elderly. The able-bodied men are, for the most part, mobilized in neighboring localities to ensure the protection of communities against possible new attacks. Some local sources also mention the involvement of armed groups alongside herders, contributing to the intensification of violence and acts of looting, including cattle theft. The administrative authorities have deployed defense and security forces, including brigade and company units, to prevent further incursions. However, the high mobility of the attackers complicates security efforts. At this stage, more than 5,800 people are estimated to be affected by this conflict, the evolution of which remains worrying. Humanitarian situation The humanitarian consequences of these clashes are significant and are reflected in: Casualties: 10 confirmed dead and 6 injured; Material losses: destruction of homes, shops, mills, motorcycles and grain stocks; Mass displacement: more than 1,000 households live in precarious conditions; Psychosocial impacts: significant trauma, especially for women and children. Displaced people are in a situation of acute vulnerability. When Red Cross teams arrived in Zigui Marba, some displaced people, fearing a new attack, initially tried to flee before being reassured by the presence of humanitarian workers. Priority needs The urgent needs identified are as follows: Shelter and essential household items: building materials, blankets, mats, mosquito nets, kitchen kits, soap; Water, hygiene and sanitation (WASH): provision of emergency latrines, access to safe drinking water, promotion of hygiene in the sites; Health: first aid, provision of medicines, psychosocial care and community support; Food security: emergency food distributions and support for the rehabilitation of agricultural and pastoral livelihoods.
actions: The sub-delegation of the FIU of Bongor also participated by making staff and equipment available.

title: Severe Hailstorm in Stepanavan

description: On 6 June 2026, at approximately 12:56 PM, a severe hailstorm struck the Stepanavan community and surrounding areas in Lori Region, Armenia. The hailstorm lasted approximately 15–20 minutes and was accompanied by exceptionally large hailstones, reportedly measuring up to 4–6 cm in diameter. The event caused extensive damage to residential properties, agricultural land, public infrastructure, vehicles, and livestock. Given the scale and severity of the impact, the Stepanavan Municipality requested support from the Armenian Red Cross Society to assist affected communities and support ongoing response efforts. Immediately following the event, the municipality activated the Community Emergency Response Group, of which ARCS is a member. ARCS joined local authorities and the Rescue Service in coordinating response efforts and gathering information on the impact of the hailstorm. Initial activities focused on identifying affected households, documenting damages, and supporting the prioritization of urgent humanitarian needs. Coordination among municipal authorities, ARCS, the Rescue Service, and other relevant stakeholders remains ongoing to monitor the evolving situation and inform response planning. 7 June 2026 update (as of 12:30 PM) Based on initial observations and information provided by local authorities, extensive damage has been reported across Stepanavan and Lori Berd communities. In the Lori Berd area, approximately 260 hectares of crops were damaged in Bovadzor, 350 hectares in Lejan, 250 hectares in Agarak, and 70 hectares in Lori Berd community. Crop losses are estimated to range between 30 and 70 per cent. More than 500 households reportedly sustained damage to roofs, windows, household plots, greenhouses, and other property. In Stepanavan, 52 individuals sustained various minor injuries, including swelling and soft tissue injuries. According to available information, none of the affected individuals sought medical treatment at health facilities. Livestock losses were also reported, including 60 lambs, four ewes, and four foals. The hailstorm caused extensive damage to private property and infrastructure in Stepanavan community. Around 950 households were reportedly affected, with damage to roofs, windows, household plots, solar energy systems, and greenhouses. Approximately 650 vehicles were damaged. Public infrastructure was also affected, including parks, recreational areas, attractions, and street lighting systems. Information collection and verification efforts are ongoing, and the number of affected households and the extent of damages may increase as additional information becomes available. ARCS, local authorities, and other relevant stakeholders continue to monitor the situation and identify priority humanitarian needs.

summary: ZMB: Epidemic - 06-2026 - Epidemic Threat
description: An Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak was confirmed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda in May 2026. The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment, although research and clinical trials on promising candidates are ongoing. The outbreak is occurring within a complex humanitarian context characterized by insecurity, high population movement, cross-border trade, and densely populated communities, increasing the risk of regional transmission. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), as of 22 May 2026, the DRC had recorded 89 confirmed Ebola cases and 823 suspected cases, while Uganda had confirmed three additional cases linked to the outbreak. WHO and partners are scaling up support to the affected governments through surveillance strengthening, contact tracing, case management, laboratory support, risk communication, community engagement, and cross-border preparedness interventions. Community engagement remains central to controlling Ebola outbreaks, as effective prevention and response depend heavily on trust, awareness, and community participation. Zambia remains at high risk of Ebola importation due to its strong socio-economic and transport linkages with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) through major border entry points and trading corridors. Although Zambia has not recorded any confirmed positive Ebola cases, two suspected cases have been reported and investigated, highlighting the continued threat of cross-border transmission. Border districts such as Kasumbalesa, Chililabombwe, Kaputa, Mpulungu, Nakonde, Solwezi, and Lusaka experience frequent population movement involving traders, truck drivers, migrant populations, and travelers from affected countries. The risk is further compounded by informal crossing points, limited infection prevention and control (IPC) capacity, and gaps in surveillance and rapid response systems. The Government of Zambia, through the Ministry of Health, has enhanced preparedness measures including surveillance strengthening, risk mapping, screening at points of entry, and readiness assessments in five provinces. However, significant gaps remain in community awareness, rapid response capacity, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, volunteer preparedness, and community-based surveillance. Drawing on the expertise in cholera response, epidemic preparedness, risk communication, and community engagement, Zambia Red Cross Society (ZRCS) seeks financial support from Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) to strengthen community-based Ebola preparedness and response interventions in high-risk border districts namely Chililabombwe. Given the continued risk of Ebola importation from neighbouring countries, there is an urgent need for increased investment in surveillance, community engagement, infection prevention and control, volunteer capacity building, and rapid response systems. Support from FCDO will enable ZRCS to complement Government efforts by enhancing preparedness at community and border levels, reducing the risk of transmission, and strengthening Zambia’s capacity to effectively prevent and respond to potential Ebola outbreaks.
actions: Incident assessment, stakeholder coordination, mitigation measures, monitoring and post-incident review.

title: Rainstorm - Riyom, Plateau state
summary: NGA: Storm Surge - 05-2026 - Rainstorm - Riyom, Plateau state
description: On the afternoon of Sunday, 31 May 2026, a severe rainstorm accompanied by a violent windstorm swept through Tom-Gangare community in Hawan Kibo of Riyom Local Government Area, Plateau State, in Nigeria’s North-Central region. The storm, which followed a prolonged and heavy downpour, generated destructive winds that tore through the rural settlement over a matter of hours, leaving a trail of widespread structural damage and deep humanitarian need in its wake. 100+ residential houses were destroyed across the community. The destruction was not limited to homes: health facilities, places of worship, educational centres and other critical community infrastructure were also damaged, stripping the population of the very services they would ordinarily rely upon in the aftermath of a disaster. The violent winds uprooted numerous mature trees, many of which crashed onto residential buildings and compounded the scale of the damage, while property and household assets worth millions of naira were reported lost. No fatalities have been reported, and this remains the single point of relief in an otherwise grave situation. However, the human impact is severe. Scores of families have been displaced and rendered homeless, and many have been left without shelter, food, clean water and other basic necessities. With homes flattened and livelihoods disrupted, affected households are now exposed to the elements and to heightened protection and health risks, particularly among women, children, older persons and persons with disabilities, who are typically the most vulnerable in the wake of sudden-onset disasters of this nature. The community sits within a wider context of recurrent storm and flood hazard across Plateau State and the Nigerian Middle Belt, a pattern that has intensified with the onset of the rainy season. Local authorities have responded at the community level: the Chairman of the Riyom Local Government Council visited the affected area to assess the extent of the damage, to sympathise with the victims, and to announce that a comprehensive damage and needs assessment would be conducted to determine the full scale of losses and to guide appropriate intervention by government and emergency-management agencies. Community stakeholders and ward representatives have appealed for urgent humanitarian support. The figures contained in this report are drawn from the rapid assessment conducted by the Nigerian Red Cross Society Riyom Division, in coordination with the State Emergency Management Agency and the local authorities.
actions: The Nigerian Red Cross Society, through its Riyom Division, responded from the earliest stage of the emergency. The Division has provided Psychosocial First Aid (PFA) to the affected families and their relatives, supported in Search and Rescue, evacuation and has been actively engaged in data collection, conducting the rapid assessment that underpins the figures contained in this report. The National Society maintains an active presence in disaster-affected communities across the country and stands ready to support the affected population in line with its auxiliary role and humanitarian mandate.
recommendations: Conduct rapid needs assessment and impact evaluation.; Activate emergency coordination mechanisms.

title: ENSO Phenomenon - El Niño Phase 2026-2027

description: In the first days of May, in most climatic regions, accumulated rainfall values are lower than normal, a closing with deficit conditions of -50% was projected for this month in the North Pacific, while the Central Pacific, South Pacific and Central Valley with -20% decrease compared to the historical average. On May 21, the IMN issued a bulletin indicating that the ENSO phenomenon (El Niño Southern Oscillation), will influence the climate of Costa Rica for the remainder of 2026, in such a way that rainfall deficits would be between 25% - 50%, in the different climatic regions of the Pacific Slope and even the Central Valley and the Northern Zone. These same regions will also be affected by temperature increases that would range between 1 - 2 degrees Celsius, which would be presented gradually. In a session of the Technical Advisory Commission on the ENSO Phenomenon (COENOS), on Wednesday, May 20, 2026, the institutions agree to declare that the ENSO phenomenon in its El Niño phase has been consolidated and is already affecting the different productive sectors of the country, so it is concluded that the climatic regions with immediate impact are the following: North Pacific, Central Pacific, Central West, Matambú, Los Santos and Capitalina. However, it is entirely possible that episodes of rainfall, typical of tropical latitudes, will occur on both slopes at any time of the year, such as those that have occurred in recent days.
actions: Monitoring of the situation and evaluation of the measures to be taken.

title: Flood Disaster in Ungheni,Călărași, Basarabeasca and Drochia
summary: MDA: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 05-2026 - Flood Disaster in Ungheni,Călărași, Basarabeasca and Drochia
description: The late-May 2026 floods were one of Moldova’s sharpest localized hydrometeorological shocks in recent months, with Călărași and Ungheni identified by the government as the most affected districts after the torrential rains of 22 May. The damage profile was dominated by flooded households, damaged roads, pressure on dams and lakes, disrupted rail traffic, and agricultural losses. The human impact was serious but uneven: the confirmed district-level reporting shows at least one death in Călărași, multiple rescue operations, households inundated in both districts, and preventive evacuation planning for additional residents at risk. As of 28 May 2026, authorities were still assessing total monetary losses, so the available picture is operational and preliminary rather than final. The heavy precipitation led to rapid water level rises in rivers, streams, and artificial reservoirs, resulting in multiple cascading impacts: Dam and embankment failures, including a reported rupture of a local dam in Hîrjauca (Călărași district), which caused sudden downstream flooding. Overflow and flooding of lakes and ponds, raising concerns about inadequate maintenance and compliance with safety standards for water basins. Flash floods affecting rural settlements, with water entering households, agricultural land, and public infrastructure. Transport disruption, including blocked roads and temporarily halted rail traffic in affected zones. Power outages and preventive disconnections in several villages due to safety risks. Soil erosion, mudflows, and damage to agricultural assets, including greenhouses and crops. The combination of saturated soils and high runoff intensity significantly amplified the destructive capacity of the floods. The strongest cross-source figures available so far show that across the wider affected zone of Călărași, Strășeni, Ungheni, and Criuleni, the floods damaged or inundated 25 localities, affected 69 households, threatened around 400 households, flooded about 400 hectares of farmland, and damaged 55 km of roads. These are important numbers because they come from the crisis-management structure after the first response phase, so they likely reflect a more consolidated operational picture than the first-night reports. However, they are not yet final compensation figures. What happened The triggering event was the 22 May storm system, which brought torrential rain, strong winds, and major water accumulation. Moldova’s authorities shifted into crisis mode, with emergency teams, police, road services, rail services, and local authorities deployed to pump water, reinforce dikes, reopen transport links, and secure high-risk areas. The government explicitly said that Călărași and Ungheni were the hardest-hit districts. gov.md IGSU The disaster affected dozens of localities across at least two key districts, with secondary impacts reported in neighboring areas. Călărași: damage analysis Călărași appears to have suffered the most intense direct household and infrastructure shock. The immediate crisis was tied to dam failure/partial rupture, especially around Hîrjauca and Mîndra, where multiple reports say over 40 households were affected. Radio Moldova also reported that in Mîndra six households were completely destroyed, while many courtyards, wells, and agricultural plots were flooded. Local officials further said that in some mayoralties 70–80% of infrastructure was affected, with bridges and local transport links damaged. Radio Moldova Radio Moldova Human impact in Călărași was severe. The government confirmed the death of a 48-year-old man in Dereneu, linked to the flooding and heavy rains. Residents were trapped in houses and vehicles, and emergency services prepared for wider preventive evacuation around Bularda/Hîrbovăț if dikes failed. One operational report noted preparations for possible evacuation of over 20 households, while a TVR Moldova report said a field camp was readied for more than 200 people in case conditions worsened. Persons at the “Codru” sanatorium were also evacuated preventively. From an analytical perspective, Călărași’s vulnerability was not just rainfall intensity. It was the combination of intense runoff, small-basin/dam failure, and cascade effects from connected lakes and drainage channels. That made the district especially prone to sudden, high-energy flooding that damaged homes, roads, yards, wells, and local agricultural assets rather than only causing shallow standing water. Ungheni: damage analysis Ungheni’s impact pattern looks broader geographically but somewhat less concentrated in destroyed homes than Călărași, at least from the public reporting now available. The government said 11 localities in Ungheni district were affected. Emergency reports and media coverage describe flooded households and basements, people stranded in vehicles or on rooftops, and drainage work in both rural settlements and the town. The key infrastructure signal in Ungheni was instability around water bodies and transport links. In Rădenii Vechi, landslides damaged two bridges in Novaia Nicolaevca. Authorities also reported an alarming situation at Lake Delia, which had accumulated water from failed upstream basins, while controlled water release operations took place near Mănoilești and Cornova to reduce pressure. Floodwater was also removed from multiple households, basements, and a kindergarten in Ungheni. Ungheni was also significant in the rescue and transport-disruption dimension. Multiple calls for help were recorded there, including incidents with people trapped in vehicles and on rooftops. Rail disruption near Pârlița temporarily stopped the Chișinău–Kyiv train with 142 passengers, illustrating that the flood impact extended beyond houses into inter-district mobility and economic connectivity. Key human impact indicators include: The public reporting allows a careful estimate of population impact, but not yet a precise district-by-district headcount. What is solid: - 69 households were actually affected across the four main districts. Moldpres - More than 400 households were considered at risk, but authorities say they were protected through dike reinforcement and drainage operations. Moldpres - In Călărași, over 40 households were flooded in Hîrjauca and Mîndra, and more than 20 households were under evacuation contingency in Bularda/Hîrbovăț. Radio Moldova Moldpres - In Ungheni, 11 localities were affected, with flooded households, a kindergarten, damaged bridges, and multiple rescue incidents. What remains uncertain: - There is no finalized official headcount of people directly affected in Călărași and Ungheni alone. - There is also no final published monetary damage estimate yet. - One media roundup referred to two deaths across Călărași and Ungheni, but the clearest official district-level confirmation currently available is one death in Dereneu, Călărași. Based on household estimates and rural population density, the directly affected population is estimated at several hundred people, while the indirectly affected population (service disruption, mobility constraints, power outages, and economic losses) likely extends to several thousand residents across the two districts. Casualties and Vulnerable Groups At least one fatality was reported in Călărași district (Dereneu village) as a result of flooding-related incidents. Preventive evacuations were conducted, including from areas near the Codru sanatorium, to avoid loss of life. Vulnerable groups include rural households, elderly populations in isolated villages, and communities located near water basins and low-lying river valleys. The main analytical conclusion is that Călărași suffered the more destructive household and infrastructure blow, while Ungheni experienced wider spatial disruption and acute water-management stress, especially around lakes, slopes, and transport corridors. This distinction matters for recovery planning: Călărași needs more household reconstruction and local infrastructure repair, while Ungheni may need stronger slope stability, drainage, and basin management measures. Why these floods were so damaging The event shows a classic compound local flood pattern: 1. Short, intense rainfall 2. Overflow and failure pressure on ponds/dikes 3. Cascade effects between connected basins 4. Localized flash flooding in villages 5. Secondary impacts on roads, rail, wells, and farmland That combination explains why relatively small localities could suffer disproportionate destruction. In other words, this was not only a “rain event”; it was a water-retention and drainage system stress event. Authorities at national and local levels activated emergency mechanisms: Deployment of emergency response teams, firefighters, police, and road services. Continuous water pumping, reinforcement of embankments, and clearance of blocked infrastructure. High-level field visits by government officials, with ongoing coordination between ministries. Ongoing damage assessment processes, as many impacts remain under evaluation due to receding waters. The situation remains dynamic, with residual risks linked to: further rainfall forecasts, saturated ground conditions, structural vulnerabilities of water retention infrastructure. On 26 May 2026, the leadership of the Red Cross Society of Moldova (MRCS), together with regional directors from affected districts, conducted a field visit to Călărași district, one of the areas most severely impacted by recent flooding caused by heavy rainfall. The mission aimed to assess field conditions, identify urgent community needs, and determine appropriate humanitarian support. In Dereneu village, discussions with local authorities focused on flood impacts, damage to households, and coordination of emergency response efforts. The MRCS team also met with a bereaved family affected by the disaster to express institutional solidarity and assess immediate support needs. In the Bularda area, the delegation met with GIES (IGSU) emergency responders engaged in flood protection works, including embankment reinforcement using sandbags and the creation of diversion channels. The team also reviewed ongoing emergency infrastructure measures and identified operational needs for responders and affected communities. In Mândra village, field visits to affected households were carried out in coordination with social workers to assess urgent humanitarian needs, including material assistance and psychosocial support for vulnerable families. MRCS reaffirmed its continued presence in the affected areas and its commitment to provide humanitarian assistance, psychosocial support, and coordination with local authorities. The organization emphasized its role in strengthening local response capacity and community resilience in line with its humanitarian mandate. By 27–28 May, authorities indicated that the immediate flood danger had been reduced through dike strengthening, pumping, and controlled drainage, but the recovery phase was only beginning. The local emergency commissions were still inventorying losses, and support from local budgets plus central government top-ups was being considered. That means the current picture is best read as initial impact analysis, not a completed loss-and-needs assessment. Călărași and Ungheni were the epicenter of Moldova’s May 2026 flood emergency. Călărași suffered the heaviest direct destruction to homes and local infrastructure, including dam-related flooding and at least one confirmed death. Ungheni experienced widespread multi-locality flooding, bridge damage, water-basin instability, and transport disruption. The total economic loss is still being assessed, but the event already shows a major combined impact on households, roads, farmland, and local resilience. Update on situation (15.06.2026) The destruction escalated during the weekend of June 6–7, when rescuers executed 37 emergency missions in a single day. During this wave, 100 households were hit in Gangura (Ialoveni district) and 20 households in Gribova (Drochia district). As the heavy rains persisted into June 11–12, emergency teams launched over 30 rapid interventions , including 25 missions in the Telenești district alone to pump out flooded cellars and tow stranded vehicles. The infrastructure also suffered heavy damage. The extreme water pressure completely ruptured 1 protection dam in Hîrjauca, damaged 2 bridges due to landslides in Rădenii Vechi, and temporarily halted 3 trains as mud and debris covered the railway tracks. As of 7 June 2026, the Red Cross Society of Moldova had provided humanitarian assistance to 176 families affected by severe weather conditions in the districts of Călărași, Strășeni, Ungheni, Basarabeasca, Drochia. In Călărași District, 160 families from the localities of Bularda, Dereneu, Hîrjăuca, Mândra, and Bravicea received 1,220 essential relief items. The shipment included large quantities of bed linen sets (340), blankets (170), hygiene kits (170), water filters (170), water filter cartridges (170), pillows (30), and other essential household items, benefiting families in Bularda, Dereneu, Hîrjăuca, Mândra, and Bravicea. In Greblești village, Strășeni District, 11 families received more than 120 essential relief items, including blankets, duvets, pillows, bed linen, water filters, kitchenware, and hygiene products, helping them meet their immediate post-disaster needs. Basarabeasca District received a total of 330 relief items, including 66 units each of five categories of essential supplies: hygiene kits, bed linen sets, blankets, cooking pots, and water filters. Drochia District received 96 relief items across eight different categories, making it the most diverse distribution in terms of item variety. The assistance included hygiene kits, bed linen sets, blankets, cooking pots, water filters, water filter cartridges, pillows, and bed covers. Cornova, Ungheni District, 5 affected families received 65 relief items for vulnerable households. In addition to standard relief supplies such as hygiene kits, bed linen sets, blankets, water filters, cartridges, and pillows, the distribution also included kitchenware items, specifically pots with lids, frying pans with lids, and medium-sized cookware sets. In addition to supporting affected households, the Red Cross Society of Moldova also assisted emergency response operations. In Bularda, where reinforcement works were carried out to strengthen a protective dam and prevent further flooding, food supplies were provided to the personnel involved in these operations. Assessments continue in the affected communities, and the organization is closely monitoring the evolving situation and the needs of the population. Subject to available resources, the response will be expanded through the distribution of essential household items, hygiene and cleaning kits, and other forms of assistance for the most vulnerable families.
actions: Since the onset of the flooding emergency, the Red Cross Society of Moldova (MRCS) has been actively engaged in field presence, coordination, and rapid needs identification in the most affected districts, including Călărași and Ungheni. During the latest field engagement, MRCS leadership and regional teams conducted on-site visits to affected communities to assess humanitarian needs, strengthen coordination with local authorities and emergency services, and identify priority support areas. Special attention was given to severely affected households, vulnerable families, and cases requiring immediate assistance, including psychosocial support. Based on ongoing assessments, MRCS is preparing targeted assistance for approximately 200 affected households, including the provision of non-food items (NFIs), basic household support, and tailored assistance packages (PFA) where required for the most vulnerable cases. In parallel, the National Society has reinforced coordination with all relevant decision-making actors, including local public authorities, emergency response services, and social assistance structures, to ensure an integrated and timely response. MRCS remains actively present in the field and continues to adjust its response based on evolving needs, with a focus on humanitarian relief, psychosocial support, and strengthening local response capacities.
